speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES    ANNOUNCEMENT OF REPAYMENT OF LOAN
speechtext:
I wish to announce that all advances made by Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to finance the construction of the western section of the all-Canadian natural gas pipe line have been repaid. Although under the provisions of the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation Act the corporation has been authorized to make loans to Trans-Canada of 90 per cent of the cost of construction of the western section or $80 million, whichever was the lesser, the actual advances made pursuant to the indenture of mortgage dated June 7, 1956, amounted to $49,750,000. The amount repaid to the corporation was $50,716,603.03, made up as follows: advances, $49,750,000; interest at 5 per cent on advances, $880,071.40; costs of the crown corporation relating to the advances, $86,531.63, making a total of $50,716,603.03.
The Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation, in addition to administering the loan to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to finance the western section, is responsible for the construction of the northern Ontario section of the pipe line which will extend approximately 675 miles from the Manitoba-Ontario border to the vicinity of Kapuskasing.

Mr. Pearson also proposes that United Nations police units deploy along the demarcation line to prevent raids from either side. He suggested it should be agreed there would be no interference with the innocent passage of ships through the gulf of Aqaba. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member notified me that he intended to ask a question on this matter and also the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) has indicated his continuing interest. Perhaps my reply could provide both them and the house with the information.
A strike deadline in this dispute was set by the union for 7.30 a.m. yesterday and at that hour plant operations started to shut down on a progressive basis as previously arranged between the union and the company in the event that a settlement of the dispute


was not effected by that time. Under this arrangement, the strike does not become fully effective until March 4.
However, by the time the strike deadline had been reached, Mr. Eric Taylor, the commissioner whom I had appointed to mediate the dispute, had succeeded in narrowing down the disputed issues from approximately sixty to seven. This had been accomplished by almost continuous negotiations over a period of several days prior to the strike deadline. Yesterday morning, after an all-night session, negotiations were adjourned until ten o'clock this morning when Mr. Taylor was to make an effort to conciliate the remaining issues in dispute. I have every reason to hope that the full effects of a strike will be averted.

I do not know whether the second cook was there at that time, but I suspect not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This motion provides for the setting up of a committee on estimates, the original of which was set up two years ago. It is in the light of the experience of those two years that I intend to direct my remarks today.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Before the Leader of the Opposition proceeds any further, may I ask all hon. members who wish to vacate the house to do so immediately so that the Leader of the Opposition may be heard in an orderly fashion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think, in the light of that experience, it can be stated that on the basis of the present powers provided for within this resolution this committee will not discharge the responsibilities that it could discharge if given the opportunity. The indications are that this year, when the sup-plementaries are introduced, Canada's expenditures will exceed anything in our history. This committee was set up for the purpose of making recommendations and suggestions as to economies, if any, that might be secured by reason of examination and discussion.

We can go back to 1921 when a similar matter was first suggested, and at that time Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux pointed out that there was a very pronounced need on the part of this parliament to examine into expenditures; that the ordinary media for the examination of expenditures were insufficient for the purpose and had been proven more or less ineffective over the years. He said this at page 2193 of Hansard for that year in introducing a resolution in the following terms:
... in order to co-ordinate and expedite the business of parliament in a more intelligent and practical way, the estimates of the various departments should, before being laid on the table, be scrutinized by a special committee of the house, where officers would be summoned to appear with plans and reports bearing on each appropriation.
I particularly emphasize the latter words of the resolution, "where officers would be summoned to appear with plans and reports bearing on each appropriation." As I see the situation today there are three controls on expenditures. The first is the cabinet, the second is the treasury board and the third is the committee of supply. The experience of all of us, I am sure, has been that no adequate examination is possible in the committee of supply; it is almost totally ineffectual. Today expenditures are fabulous in amount and, except for ministers in the government, there are no adequate research opportunities whereby parliament may properly discharge its responsibilities. There is no adequate, indeed, in many cases, no examination of the expenditures of that vast, sprawling empire of crown corporations which is in existence today. When I say that, I am not unmindful of the fact that there is an examination of the C.B.C. from time to time, the Canadian National Railways and the Trans-Canada Air Lines. But outside of these, and an auditor's examination by the Auditor General, there is a completely ineffectual examination of crown corporations whose expenditures run into the millions and millions of dollars.
The first estimates committee was set up in 1955, as I said a moment ago. Has it proven effectual? What have been its shortcomings? It has had no power to call for persons, papers or records. It has had placed before it the evidence permitted by the minister of the crown for the particular department being investigated. Some might say this committee could go into details. No one is so naive as not to realize that the evidence is not given, whenever an examination is commenced that in any way may lead to politically detrimental circumstances in so far as the government is concerned. What evidence has been brought before the committee in the past few years
Committee on Estimates has been that which the government was prepared to present. I am not going into details. The experience of the previous year was set out by a number of our members in 1956, and in particular I would refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops, at page 1639 of Hansard for February 28, 1956. He set out the difficulties in connection with the committee and its operations. What the committee has done, in effect, is to get the people as a whole to believe that effective work is being done when, in point of fact, being unable to call witnesses, it is completely ineffectual in the achievement of its purposes.
In so far as an examination of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration was concerned the minister himself set cut in detail on February 24, at page 10 of the committee proceedings for 1955, his ideas as to the powers of this committee and the manner in which those powers should be exercised. He said this:
The view 1 have taken on what I should do is to use my own judgment when a question is asked as to whether it is the type of question I should take the responsibility of answering myself or the type of question I should ask one of the officers of the department to answer.
I do not intend myself to answer questions which do not involve policy and which do involve detail, because I think it would be quite ridiculous for me to turn to one of these gentlemen here and ask him to whisper the answer to me. He is far more capable of giving the answer himself because I do not pretend to be an expert on the details of the department. However, I would like it clearly understood that any question which I wish to answer myself X have the right to answer exclusively.
Well, Mr. Speaker, can you conceive of a committee effectually examining expenditures when a question is asked which, in the opinion of the minister, he ought to answer, and while the civil servants have the information, the answer is given by him. It is because of that fact and the attitude taken by the government in the past few years that the committee, which was born in circumstances of hope, has not achieved anything like the position of responsibility that its opportunities provided. You say to me, what is the alternative? Well, I do not intend to go into particulars regarding the United Kingdom committee, but that committee was set up in 1912 by the then Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Lloyd George. That committee consists of 36 members. It is broken up into subcommittees, and it examines departments without warning them in advance, and it does not allow the minister to prevent witnesses coming before it. I would ask, sir, does anyone in the practice of law agree that if a court was convened-and I see a difference between this and a court-and the only evidence that could be introduced would be

Committee on Estimates that which one or other of the parties decided was the type of evidence which would not be hurtful to him, that indeed would be the evidence? That is the position here. The minister sits on the committee, or at least the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) sat on the committee; whatever questions were asked that in his opinion might be construed as detrimental, or at least bore that suggestion, a reading of the evidence before the committee indicates the degree to which its powers of investigation were emasculated. I believe that, in the light of the experience of the last two years, the criticisms of this party have been proven to be correct.
We suggest that the estimates committee should be empowered to do those things which the committee in the United Kingdom has discharged now for some 45 years. It is an effective job that the United Kingdom committee has performed. It has made examinations year by year; it has investigated various departments of government without notice in advance. After all, if auditors are sent in to make an examination no notice is sent in advance in order to provide an opportunity for glossing over circumstances which otherwise would be revealed.
I wish that the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) were in the house today. Last year he set out in very great detail, and most wisely, the terms upon which the committee should be set up and indicated how ineffectual it would be unless it had the power to send for documents and secure witnesses.
All of us desire to make parliament effective. All, I think, realize the degree to which parliament has changed in its attitude in the last 15 years, or particularly following the first war and since the second great war.
I do not propose to quote from the articles in the Queen's Quarterly, the winter of 1957 edition, the focus on parliament, in which a series of contributors have given their views on parliament. It must be authentic because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is one of those who made contributions to the article. However, it is not from him that I intend to quote because what he dealt with does not apply to the question of an estimates committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, he dealt with the estimates committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I will allow the minister to deal With that when he speaks. I am going to quote an independent witness,-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Like Michener.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
-not one who is biased in any way, but one who still enjoys to a

high degree the appreciation of the government and who within the last few days has received an appointment on a commission to investigate the situation of Newfoundland in confederation. I refer to John Deutsch who over the years held high positions in the civil service of this country. He has written an article entitled "Parliament and the Civil Service", and has shown the difficulties of parliament and the degree to which in the passing years ministers of the crown have become, as they read those daily statements, simply the means of articulating someone else's preparations. He says this:
Traditionally parliament's ultimate control over the civil service and the executive has lain in its power respecting expenditures. The power remains, but its exercise has undergone important changes. There has been much comment on the fact that in practice parliament finds it convenient to spend a large part of its time on general debates and the consideration of broad objectives and issues which are congenial to the talents of the members and arouse some measure of public interest. There is little or no manifestation of general public interest in the details of technical operations which today constitute so large a part of the work of government and the civil service.
In a paragraph further on he goes on to say:
In order to bring parliament into closer touch with the operation of the civil service it has been proposed that parliament should set up a considerable number of functional committees each of which would make it its business to become thoroughly familiar with, and to exercise surveillance over, a particular area of government activity.
Having said that, he sets out the obvious answers that such a system might not be effectual under the British form of parliamentary government, but he says that something must be done to bring about an improvement in the information available to parliament. He goes on to say:
One step to this end, which would be in harmony with the principles of our parliamentary system, would be the development of a procedure for a regular annual review of the administrative operations of government by a suitable parliamentary body.
That is exactly what we have been asking for over the years. Today, with the estimates being brought in in the latter days of the session, it is possible if not probable that millions of dollars that have no justification in the estimates pass in the rush that takes place at the end of each session. There is today no way whereby it is possible for parliament properly to discharge its functions in the examination of supply. If you go back to the debates of 1868, 1869, 1870, 1871 and 1872, when the total expenditures of Canada amounted to from $7 million to $14 million, you will find that there was an intense examination of detail. That is past today. For one reason, the volume of expenditures, the mass of detail in the Auditor

General's report and the extensive nature of the estimates preclude any careful examination. Mr. Deutsch who occupied some of the highest positions in Canada's civil service and who today is a professor in the University of British Columbia-a man who knows- realizes that something must be done, but not through a committee such as this estimates committee which is to be the watchdog of the treasury and is muzzled in advance by being denied the right to call witnesses. His suggestion is this:
Under this proposal a committee of the House of Commons on which there is wide representation (possibly the existing public accounts committee with some modifications) would bring before it each year during the course of the session, all of the permanent civil service heads of departments and agencies to give an accounting of their administrative operations during the previous year, and to submit to examination thereon.
If that suggestion came from a member of the opposition it would possibly be said that it was an interference with the authority of the cabinet, with their responsibility incident to being Her Majesty's advisers. But here is the advice of a great Canadian, one who has over the years received plaudits from members of the government. He is suggesting that today it is needful that parliament have an opportunity of examining senior civil servants, heads of departments and agencies to give an accounting of their administrative operations. He also said:
The important point is that this review should be conducted regularly, thoroughly and comprehensively . . . While attempts to wring indiscretions from civil servants might be good political sport, concentration on this would quickly degrade the work of the committee. In order to be effective the committee would have to make a purposeful effort to review, comprehend, appraise, and finally to prepare a useful report on the administration of government activities. If this were done members of parliament would have an opportunity to get a much better appreciation of what they are expected to control.
In other words there would be parliamentary control in the examination of estimates and parliament would be made aware of the basis upon which the various estimates had been recommended. Mr. Speaker, I think that this is one of the most challenging recommendations that anyone connected with the civil service has made heretofore. Mr. Deutsch speaks not as a partisan of any party but as a partisan for a rejuvenated parliament that will discharge its responsibilities.
Throughout the years I have said-and I repeat it now-that there is today no means whereby expenditures can be examined. There is no means available. In the first place, members of the opposition naturally have not that research knowledge which is necessary; they have not available to them the civil
Committee on Estimates service. They are obliged to depend on information that comes in that desultory way that has existed throughout the years. Gladstone once said: It is more difficult to save a shilling than to spend a million. An estimates committee, properly set up, could bring about savings in this country which would be beneficial not only to the departments concerned but above all to the taxpayers.
Up to the present time, with the exception of that committee which was set up during the days of the war-I refer to the war expenditures committee-there has been no serious endeavour through the years to meet this problem of a careful examination and scrutiny coupled with the necessary recommendations as to the achievement of savings. During the war the committee on war expenditures was set up. It met throughout the years. It saved Canada tens of millions of dollars. The members of that committee worked not for any political purpose but in order to discharge their responsibilities. That committee had power. That committee called witnesses before it. That committee became effective.
The committee that is now being set up under this resolution is but a copy of the one that has been in existence for two years. In the light of that experience I say that unless it has the power to call witnesses and to ask for papers, it is nothing but a sham and a delusion. It promises great things but it is shackled in advance by its lack of powers. In the light of that experience, Mr. Speaker, and in order to make it effectual, it is my purpose to move an amendment as follows. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming):
That the motion be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"And that the said committee have power to send for persons, papers and records."

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the motion of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to establish once again the estimates committee. We are also pleased that the leader of the official opposition has moved an amendment which I believe is identical with an amendment that was moved last year when the same motion was before the house. Even as we supported the amendment last year we shall support the amendment that has now been proposed because we feel that this committee should not be denied a power that is enjoyed by all the standing committees of this house, namely the power to send for persons, papers and records.
We think that the last word has not been said, Mr. Speaker, on the question of how parliament should operate in pursuit of Its

Committee on Estimates functions with regard to public expenditures. We have a public accounts committee, we have the committee of supply and for the last few years we have had the estimates committee. Yet I think that no one on the government side or on the opposition side of the house would be so foolish' as to assert that we have yet got on top of this terrific problem of managing the huge expenditures which come under the jurisdiction of parliament.
We hope that the government, complacent though it may be about some other matters, will not take the view that it has done all it needs to do in agreeing to the appointment of this committee. We believe that serious study should be given by the government to suggestions such as those made by John Deutsch, to which the Leader of the Opposition has referred already, and to suggestions in other articles on the question of parliamentary control of expenditures which appear from time to time and which are written by those who have studied this whole question, particularly some of those in our universities.
As John Deutsch points out in the article to which reference has been made already, the problem facing parliament today in this respect is indeed a tremendous one. I was going to cite certain quotations in Professor Deutsch's article but the ones I have marked are the ones the Leader of the Opposition has quoted already and I will not take the time of the house to repeat them at this time. However, I would point out that he does say on page 568 of the current issue of the Queen's Quarterly that the difficulty confronting parliament lies essentially in the problem of how to control this vast machine, including the executive which directs it. It is on the basis of that premise that Professor Deutsch made the suggestion which has been quoted already, namely that there should be set up in parliament a committee which would make it possible for senior civil servants to be called before it for proper examination, not just for the purpose of ferreting out tidbits that are interesting to political parties but so that members of parliament generally might get a better grasp of the problem that is ours in controlling the huge expenditures of a federal government.
I was interested in the interjection made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) when the Leader of the Opposition referred to the current issue of Queen's Quarterly. The Minister of Finance assured us that he had had something to say in his article about the estimates committee. That is right, he did. It is not very long so I think I can put it on the record. I find that the minister referred to the estimates committee in two places. At pages 544 and 545 he had this to say:

During the last two sessions the proceedings (questions and answers) in the estimates committee have covered eight of the twenty departments of government, taking approximately 1,700 printed pages. The proponents of this system have argued that it would reduce the time taken in the house for the consideration of these departments, but experience has shown that the opposite has been true. However, it is still too early for a final judgment, particularly as the departments which have been examined in detail by the estimates committee have been in some cases quite contentious. One may be able to judge the results better when more departments have had detailed scrutiny.
The other reference which the Minister of Finance made in his article to the estimates committee is on page 547 as follows:
The estimates committee will also have to prove its worth either as a time-saver or as a more efficient check on public spending.
We cannot help but agree with the proposition the Minister of Finance lays down that the estimates committee should prove a check on public spending and I suppose from the standpoint of personal convenience we should go along with the idea that the estimates committee should be a time-saver. However, it seems to me that that is the fundamental fallacy in the approach of the Minister of Finance to the whole question of the business of parliament. His preoccupation seems to be to get the sessions over. It seems to me that that is quite contrary to the conclusion that John Deutsch comes to at the end of his article. He recognizes that the committee structure which he proposes will not have the effect of shortening the session. In fact he says this:
The adoption of proposals along these lines, would, of course, mean more work for an already burdened parliament. However, this is basically a matter of the most effective allocation of time. What is needed is an allocation of time and an organization of work which is in harmony with the realities of government today. These realities have to be faced if parliament is to maintain its proper relationship to the executive and the civil service.
It seems to me that that is the basic difference between the approach of the Minister of Finance and that of Professor Deutsch, namely that the Minister of Finance as house leader thinks in terms of ways and means of getting the sessions over with as little discussion as possible. Professor Deutsch thinks in terms of the problem on the doorstep of parliament as being such a gigantic one that we need a more up-to-date committee structure to cope with these matters. I think we would all go along with Professor Deutsch's suggestion that one of the needs is the establishment of a committee structure which will acquaint all members of parliament more fully with the functions of various departments and the job that we have in hand.

When one looks at these articles by professors dealing with the job confronting parliament he realizes that the committee structure we have falls short of what is needed. However, we welcome the attempt at least to move in that direction by having a committee such as is now proposed, namely an estimates committee. Most of us have had the experience of serving on this committee at one time or another. In fact I suppose more hon. members have had a chance to serve on the estimates committee than on other committees by reason of the fact that the tendency of all parties is to rotate their members on that committee as different departments come before it.
It was my experience to be a member of the committee for a while last year when we had the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare before us. To me it was a good committee, but hardly an estimates committee in the terms of the meaning of that word. Actually it was dealing with the estimates of that particular department last year shortly after the federal government had made its proposal to the provinces for a national hospitalization insurance scheme. I understand that this has now been agreed to by five provinces. For the most part in that committee we were discussing this proposal. I have no complaint that we dealt with health insurance while I was on that committee; that was what some of us wanted. While we did deal with some other matters, mainly it was that subject that was before us at that time. That was all to the good.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt to ask the hon. member before he sits down what he would have discussed if that matter had not been chosen?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance knows that I am not complaining that we had the committee and were able to use it for that purpose. What I am suggesting is that partly because we do not have the power to send for persons, papers and records, partly because we have not yet looked seriously at the practice in the United Kingdom where the committee is more evenly balanced with a member of the opposition party acting as chairman, we have not moved in the direction of a committee the purpose of which would be a parliamentary duplicate, if I may call it that, of the treasury board. It seems to me that something like that is needed in our parliamentary set-up.
I recognize the constitutional arguments that will be put forward based on the fact that the government is responsible for all expenditures and therefore the treasury board has to do that job under the aegis of the government. But if parliament ultimately has to pass the
Committee on Estimates estimates, and even though the recommendations are made by the government parliament has to take the final responsibility in all financial measures, it seems to me that we must find ways and means of becoming more fully informed in order to be in a better position to do our job with respect to these estimates.
I say quite frankly to the Minister of Finance that this is not criticism of him or of the government itself, it is simply stating the plain fact that we in the parliament of Canada have not yet thought in these terms in relation to public expenditures the way they have in the parliament of the United Kingdom. I hope that further thought will be given to the nature and to the set-up of this committee. Maybe it is an experiment -an idea that will not work out. Maybe what we need is to revise the structure of the public accounts committee; maybe we need to put the two together. But it would be my hope that further thought might be given to this question so that we might yet find a better way of investigating and scrutinizing public expenditures than we have at the present time either in the public accounts committee or in the estimates committee.
The estimates committee would be a little better if the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) were adopted, and we shall therefore support it. The estimates committee is to be set up again this year, and even on the old basis certain departments are to be referred to that committee. We suggest that all of us in this house, both on the government side and among the opposition parties, should be giving further thought as to what might be a still better way for parliament to scrutinize and supervise public expenditures.
Mt. G. W. McLeod (Okanagan-Revelsloke):
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words, very briefly, on this subject. We were very glad to see that this committee would be set up again this year, and I will say at the outset that we are also pleased to see the amendment by the Leader of the Opposition. I had intended to make, and I will include in my remarks, a few suggestions to that effect.
During the past few years it has been my privilege to sit on this committee, and I do believe it has proven a worth-while instrument by means of which parliament can make a closer and more careful study of the spending of the money entrusted to it. After all, I believe one of the most important functions of parliament should be to see that money taken from the people of Canada to finance their government is

Committee on Estimates spent in a way that will serve their best interests. Today, when our yearly expenditure is in the neighbourhood of $5 billion, it is doubly important to do this. We heard in this house in the not too distant past the words "What is a million?" and I think that a little more careful scrutiny would make sure that that phrase is not taken too literally by the departments administering the affairs of this government.
During some of these committee meetings I have been, at times, beset with a feeling of frustration. We realize the shortcomings of the procedure, and we realize that there is room for improvement. However, I think an improvement is quite possible, and that with more experience we shall be able to get down more effectively to the job which is entrusted to us, and become more efficient in discharging it.
We must come closer to the problems of administration within the department under review, and I believe we should get to know any flaws in the method of operation and in the handling of public funds. I believe we should be able to come to certain conclusions as a result of our work, and that we should be able to make suggestions with reasonable assurance that those suggestions would be listened to by the officials of the departments under review.
There is another thing which troubles me, more perhaps than anything else-the fact that these committee meetings have sometimes tended to become a sounding board for what might be called political discussions on policy. I do not believe that the functions of this committee are to discuss policy, and this is something which we should bear in mind as we enter upon another period of the work of this particular committee. It should not be used as a political medium in order to try to embarrass the administrators of the department under examination. After all, Mr. Speaker, these administrators and departmental officials are merely carrying out the laws and regulations laid down by this parliament, and if we believe it is necessary to change those laws or regulations the place to talk about that, and the place to have such action recommended and taken, is in this house and not in the estimates committee.
I would, therefore, suggest that the committee, after it has completed its work in examining the estimates of any department, should present certain recommendations to parliament in accordance with its findings, and that those suggestions should be accepted by this house and by the government as indicating a need for definite action along the lines recommended by the committee.


As to the terms of reference, I would suggest that this committee be given very wide scope, and that in accordance with the resolution it be "empowered to send for persons, papers and things." Then, Mr. Speaker, once this committee has been set up, and once the terms of reference have been set forth, I suggest that the committee should carry on strictly within the limits of those terms of reference, and that the members should do their utmost to make a careful and thorough study of the expenditures presented to them by the departments under review.

Mr. Speaker, I will take a few moments in which to express my views in connection with the setting up of this committee.
In the short time during which I have been a member of the House of Commons I have sat on a good many different committees and I have spent many hours in committee work. I have heard members of the official opposition proposing, week after week, the setting up of committees for particular purposes, I have sat on some of the committees whose establishment was urged by hon. members of the opposition, and my own experience has been that after the committees are set up it is almost impossible to get a quorum. The hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. McLeod) will, I think, agree with me that only last year it proved a problem on many occasions to get a quorum in our committees, and I think it will be found, if you look back into the records, that the quorum of every committee has been quite substantially reduced in the last two or three sessions of this parliament.
The criticism in connection with this particular committee, of which I have been a member, is the fact that the minister himself is dealing with his own estimates. With that I agree 100 per cent because I believe the minister is the man who should be dealing with his estimates, and from my experience of that committee I can say there has not been one iota of evidence withheld from members; any information they have requested has been provided without any hesitation at all. Great emphasis has been placed on the fact that these committees can save millions of dollars for the taxpayers. I must again speak frankly and say that I find that the opposition members do make every effort to create the impression among the general public that their job here is to save dollars for the taxpayers, but if you take Hansard you will find that what they are actually doing is recommending the expenditure of a great deal more money than is covered by the estimates. We have been sitting here for

a very short time, six or seven weeks, and I have gone over the records hurriedly. If the suggestions already made by the official opposition were taken seriously by the government they would amount to $2 billion added to our expenditures this year.
Nonsense.

No nonsense. I can give the hon. member the exact figures if he would like to have them. I pick up today's order paper and look at notices of motions. There is one to increase the pensions of civil servants. There is another to accelerate activities in the field of research. Every single item under notices of motions involves an increase in expenditure and nine out of ten of them come from the official opposition.
I believe it is nearly time that we took this matter seriously and those who really believe we should save dollars should practise exactly what they preach. When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke a few moments ago he said that it was harder to save a shilling than to spend a million. I agree with that statement. If the records of those who have been members of these committees dealing with the estimates are checked it will be found that when they take part in discussion in the House of Commons-and I defy any member of the house to find anything that will contradict this statement-for every suggestion of lesser expenditure there will be 100 recommendations for greater expenditure.
You were never more ridiculous in your life.
I should like the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) to get up and show me one case where he ever asked that expenditure be curtailed in his own constituency.
Just last year-

Just get up and I
will give you the floor.

speechtext: May I remind the hon. member that if he gives the floor I will recognize the hon. member for Eglinton.
I do not believe the hon. member for Eglinton wants the floor.
I will be very glad to take the floor if the hon. member is prepared to yield the floor on the terms indicated.

The hon. member who has just interrupted is the very same gentleman who stood before the Tory convention held a few months ago where everything that could be thought of was promised the people of Canada. That was the start for the election, and that same gentleman
Committee on Estimates will stand up on platforms all across the country and say that the people of New Brunswick are not being treated fairly, the South Saskatchewan dam should be built, and anything else that has been suggested involving the expenditure of money he will endorse. But at the same time we have a very serious obligation in connection with the taxpayers' dollars. If those in the official opposition are really serious in what they are saying then when the estimates come before the house again, whenever it is, let them get up and say, for example, here is an expenditure of $250,000 in my constituency and I believe it should be cut out. Let them say that they are prepared to save the taxpayers' dollars. In my experience extending over 12 years I have yet to hear one member of the opposition even suggest the saving of a single dollar.
I remember that when we were dealing with the estimates in the last session of parliament I sat here day after day until I got disgusted and got to my feet. There was one item in the agricultural estimates and the hon. gentleman who is the agricultural expert of the official opposition took 15 minutes of the time of the house to find out why an expenditure had been cut from $165,000 to $150,000. He was bitterly opposed to a cut of $15,000 in that item. If it had been an increase he would have endorsed it.
I believe we must take this matter more seriously. We must be honest with ourselves. If we set up this committee to save dollars, then let us take the same attitude when the estimates are before the house as we take in the committee because while the public reads Hansard and the press publishes what is said here the public do not read the records of these committees. Why go to a committee and slug it out day after day and try to make the people believe they are saving money and then get up on their feet when the estimates are brought back to this chamber and say that they are very sorry because the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) has neglected to supply the cash to build this building in a certain constituency or a breakwater somewhere else or a railroad somewhere else?
They are disappointed that the government has not announced an increase in old age pensions. On public platforms and the radio they accuse the government of neglecting to increase family allowances. If they really want to save money let them get up on their feet and show us where we can save it. If I am a member of the committee when it is set up I hope we will be able to get a quorum without keeping the minister and others who want to get the work of

Committee on Estimates parliament completed sitting there hour after hour waiting for enough members of the official opposition to make a quorum.
