-who wants speed when he is not particularly concerned with affairs but does not want speed with respect to anything else on which he might feel he should take more time. If I may, let me refer briefly to the debate which has occurred on every occasion when this matter has been before the house. I know that hon. members do not want to re-read what I said when I moved the appointment of an estimates committee two years ago. If they will do so, however, they will find that I set out there what I thought the principles of an estimates committee on an experimental basis should be which would result in the obtaining of information such as hon. members said they did not have the time in the house to obtain.
I repeat that because that was the basis on which we thought the estimates committee might start, namely, that hon. members said that late in the session they did not have time to consider in detail the estimates in the blue book. They said that they did not feel like embarrassing themselves or the minister concerned by asking questions about a very small item which might only apply to their particular riding and not to the country as a whole but that if they had the time in a committee room they could take all the time they wanted on little questions of that kind that were of considerable moment to them but not perhaps to other members of the committee of supply.
In addition, I am free to confess that hon. members opposite, particularly in the official opposition, thought that if they had another chance at a fishing expedition they might conceivably find some basis of complaint against government spending, this despite the fact they had gone through three or four years of trying to do it in the Department of National Defence and had got absolutely nowhere with their fishing expedition.
We have had two years' experience with this committee. It is not doing anything that


it was thought it possibly might do except to-place on the record a lot of information which would not have been placed on the record if questions had been confined to the committee of supply. No member opposite, except the last member who spoke for the Social Credit party, went so far as to say that he was reasonably well pleased with the committee. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is pleased with it to some extent but it would appear that the official opposition is not pleased at all.
The reasons are clear. Last year, when the national health estimates were considered by the committee, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre concentrated his attention on an item of $124,000 out of a total of $900 million for the purpose of talking about something that was not in the estimates, namely, health insurance. This is the kind of action that is probably all right if one understands the rules of the game, but if this is intended to be a critical examination of estimates rather than a demand for a change in policy that kind of action ought to be taken in the House of Commons and not in a committee which asserts to be an estimates committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I ask the question not to deny what he has just said at all, but will he not admit that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) desired a discussion of health insurance and that it was he who started it in that committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have no doubt whatever that ministers tend to lean over backwards to accommodate opposition members of the committee on estimates and also anywhere else.
But let us then look at the 1800 pages of record that we have so far managed to make available to hon. members through the estimates committee. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was good enough to refer to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) and the proceedings on the estimates of that department before this committee. As I recall it that was the first department to go before the committee because the official opposition thought the department was vulnerable, if I may use that word, certainly contentious at any rate, and as I remember it the committee spent several weeks seeking not only information about expenditures but seeking

to debate policy with respect to immigration and with respect to the Indians and other persons represented in that department.
The very people who argued for the estimates committee did so on the basis that in a committee upstairs there would be no policy discussion; there would be a seeking of information on the basis of which there could be a more informed policy discussion in the committee of supply when the items came back for discussion here. Yet we find, on the basis of experience, they decided on a debate on policy in the committee itself. As I recall it we have gone through eight departments at one time or another, and some were contentious. As a matter of fact, most of them were put before the committee for that reason, so that the opposition could have more time to discuss matters that were currently interesting them. This year, if we have time and I take it that this resolution might carry, it was our intention to send at least two more departments to the committee. I had thought that perhaps during the session this fall and perhaps during the session next year, we might have been able to get around to almost all the departments at least once in that period of about four or five years.
You will see, Mr. Speaker, what is happening. We had thought, in our naive way to which the Leader of the Opposition referred, that if hon. members had a month or a month and a half of discussion, say three times a week, in a committee room upstairs, there would be some time saved in the committee of supply when we came to discuss the estimates of that particular department. As I said, in the article in the Queen's Quarterly, without really trying to prove it by a reference to hours which I could do, the result has been that we have had a longer discussion in the house in connection with every department which has gone to the estimates committee than we had the last time that department was considered in the committee of supply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Maybe that is all to the
good.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am not arguing that this
is either good or bad. I am reporting, for the moment, as I did in the Queen's Quarterly. In the Queen's Quarterly I said that this committee could prove its worth by saving time in the committee of supply or it could prove its worth by acting as a better check on government expenditures. When I moved the motion to appoint the committee two years ago, I included that as a reason why I thought there ought to be an estimates committee, and I went on to say that there
Committee on Estimates were members in every party who thought this committee would be a waste of time and would do nothing more than could be done in the committee of supply. I believe there are people in every party in the house who still feel that way on the basis of the experience we have had.
What is there to be done about this? Are we to adopt the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition that we should have a committee of the house which would, as he said, call before it the leading members of the civil service, the deputy ministers I take it or at least the chief treasury officers of the various departments, to have an annual survey of the expenditures of the government such as would suit him and suit the purposes outlined in the amendment? We have that now, Mr. Speaker. There is nothing different in the statement which was made by the Leader of the Opposition from what can be done through the public accounts committee. He has been confused himself by the difference between an estimates committee considering expenditures for the forthcoming year and a scrutiny of the expenditures which have been made in the past. When I moved the motion to appoint the estimates committee, I reminded the house they ought to keep the distinction clearly in mind. I am sorry that I have to continue quoting myself at such length. I do that because I feel a little bothered by the fact no one seems to have paid any attention to what I said at the time.
I pointed out that the kind of estimates committee hon. members seemed to have in mind was a public accounts committee on a scale which would make it all-inclusive rather than a current discussion. I gave examples of what they did in the United Kingdom. As I pointed out at that time, they appointed a committee to go to Africa to consider the peanut situation there. This took about two years. I pointed out that they selected a small item of four million pounds with regard to broadcasting and took some 18 months to make a report during which time they toured the United Kingdom. That is not what we are trying to do here; that is the work of a public accounts committee. The public accounts committee can summon people and examine them about whether or not these expenditures were properly made; whether there was waste in them and whether or not it might have been proper to do something else. All that is in the past, and we are talking today about expenditures which may be voted for the current year; whether or not the item represents a true and proper expenditure for that purpose; whether or not another item

Committee on Estimates ought to be included in the estimates. I take it that is the purpose of an estimates committee. Certainly, that is the purpose of the committee of supply. The committee of supply is set up each year for the purpose of providing money for the next fiscal year. If hon. members feel that they have the time and that as the constitution permits them to decide on what expenditures ought to be in every year, then let us concentrate on the committee of supply and do the work there. If, however, hon. members want to examine the past history of things, the public accounts committee is there for that purpose.
In between, however, there seems to be another field which I take it the Leader of the Opposition has in mind. I suppose it would mean that you select one department at the beginning of the session, take time to concentrate on it and make a report some time towards the end of that session after a careful scrutiny of the items for that department as to whether or not the expenditures ought to be as they are in the blue book. If hon. members feel that they can conduct the business of parliament in that manner, I suggest they be more specific as to how it can be done than we have heard from them so far.
I should like to say one word to follow up what has been said by the hon. member for Charlotte. I appeared before the estimates committee with my department. It is true that the Department of Finance spends something over $900 million, a large part of which is statutory. But let the house realize that that committee disposed of my $900 million in something over three and a half hours of consideration. I answered every question that was asked of me. No question was asked which would indicate that any opposition member thought there was information that was not available to him and, indeed, there is not because what information was not available at the committee hon. members can easily obtain by telephoning the officials in my department, as they know quite well. This seems to be an effort, if I may say so, by the opposition to substitute themselves for the government in taking responsibility for expenditures. If that is their purpose, it is at least a legitimate cause for discussion and recommendation. But when they recommend that, let them bring forward the appropriate amendment to the Financial Administration Act and remove from the treasury board, if you will, the authority it exercises over expenditures and substitute some other body; set up the machinery which would permit them to turn themselves into accountants and the like instead of members of parliament representing the whole of the people of Canada. The

result would be that some day we might have what happened in Washington recently, and I only mention this for information, not by way of criticism, when the budget went to congress with a statement by the secretary of the treasury that he hoped something could be done about it. This is not the policy of this government or any government that conducts itself in accordance with our constitutional procedures. The crown, through the cabinet, takes responsibility for expenditures, submits them to parliament and is ready to accept suggestions and amendments with respect to them, but in the long run accepts the responsibility for recommending them in the first place. If we make a mistake in the recommendation, then the public will visit the proper punishment upon us for that mistake. But I do not think that in the foreseeable future we shall come to the point where we shall vest in parliament as such or rather a body of parliament authority over the retaining or the ultimate passing, except with the consent of the whole of parliament, of all items to be spent in the ensuing fiscal year.
I mention what the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod) said. He said he thought this committee ought to have the privilege of recommending to civil servants present expenditures other than those referred to, or suggestions as to better administration of particular items. Surely that is the privilege of the hon. gentleman on all occasions. Surely that is what he is sent here for. We do not have to create that right by an amendment to the motion to go before a committee. I am sure my hon. friend has never been lacking in a desire to get on his feet to recommend things to cabinet, and we do give consideration to it. There is nothing mystic about it. It is part of the job, and we do not have to set up a committee and send civil servants there to listen to my hon. friend who has a telephone in his room. I did not understand him at all. I think the purpose of the committee of supply is to hear those complaints, and to hear the complaints in the estimates committee, but in the end the complaints are directed to the government and not to a particular civil servant, because he can only recommend or not recommend to his minister. In the end the minister accepts the responsibility for deciding what is done. I see my hon. friend wants to say something.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, what I did say, or what I intended to convey, and I believe it will come out that way in Hansard, is that I thought that was one of the functions of the committee that we should concentrate on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Then, I apologize. I must say I was carrying on another conversation at the time that my hon. friend was complaining. He has indicated the function of the committee, and I accept what he has said it is meant to be.
I want to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I took the responsibility for starting the estimates. committee two years ago. I would like to see it continued for at least another session, and perhaps for one or two more, to see whether in fact the providing of additional time to obtain additional information has been useful to hon. members and to the debates in the house. I did not contemplate at the time, and I do not contemplate in the immediate future at least, any alteration in the terms of reference because it would appear to me that hon. members opposite have not tried to work this committee in the manner that they might have under the terms of reference laid down two years ago. I was conscious of the complaints that have been made about attendance; I was conscious of the fact that hon. members found it inconvenient to attend the committee on many occasions and I did encourage others to attend in order that the committee might go ahead with the work it was doing.

May I ask the minister a question? Did he find that in the meetings of the committee which he and I attended there was any lack of a quorum? I have no recollection of there being a want of quorum or a want of attendance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No; I am free to confess that on the one day I appeared before the committee we had a quorum a short time after we met. There is no question about that. But I am a little afraid that a serious desire to limit expenditure is not shown either in the committee or in the house. We are spending about $5 billion. The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) has made more than one speech in the house with respect to cutting down the expenditures on publications, as I recall it, of various kinds.
Hon. members opposite have tended to speak in general terms about waste in expenditures, and I have never yet known them to rise in their places to move that a particular item be reduced, with one or two minor exceptions that I shall mention in a moment. Nor do I think, although I have not read all the 1800 pages of evidence before this committee, that very much time is put in trying to show that a particular item should not be spent. On the contrary I join with the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) in saying that almost the whole of the discussion has to do either with a search for error in
Committee on Estimates judgment, which probably is part of the purpose of the committee, or alternatively with an expenditure which is not provided for.
Now, if the house genuinely feels that large sums of money are being spent which could be saved, I can assure them that I shall be the first to hear their views thereon. We have gone to a great deal of trouble in setting up the accounts, in publishing the sheets that I hold in my hand, that are in the blue book. An obvious complaint, of course, can be the one made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre that we should not spend so many millions of dollars to publish reports; that there is a duplication here and there, as there is bound to be in any institution spending $5 billion. But when I hear hon. members opposite advocate quite large expenditures far beyond what are now being made, and in the same speech, indeed in the following sentence almost, complain about the great expenditures of government, I often wonder whether they could not put a price tag on what they are advocating and at the same time put a price tag on what they would take out of the expenditures to make up for it, or alternatively accept the responsibility for increased taxation, which would be the only result.
Now, looking at my friends of the C.C.F. party I immediately say that they have on every occasion said in the house that they are in favour of higher taxation. They have told me that they believe that government is for the purpose of certain distributions of wealth by taxation, and I exempt them from what I have said. But the official opposition, who talk about expenditures running at an unheard of rate, and at the same time recommend other expenditures, are, if I may use a colloquial term, talking out of both sides of their mouth, and it seems to me they have proven that by the use of this committee and by the evidence taken before it.

Mr. Speaker, judging by the tone of the minister's remarks, it is evident that we are not going to have very much co-operation from the government or from the minister in efforts to pare unnecessary expenditures. I am afraid it is evident also from the tone in which the minister has spoken today that there is going to be very little co-operation extended by the government to members on this side of the house, or in any quarter of the house, in their efforts to obtain information and also to scrutinize expenditures in accordance with their duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
What do you call the 1800 pages of the record except information?

Committee on Estimates
Well, I am talking about the minister's attitude today. The minister did not put 1800 pages of material on the record, today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; I am talking about the evidence in the committee.
But he did, I think, exhibit an attitude in his remarks today which does not reflect any co-operation or a co-operative approach to the matter I have reference to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Hoping that you will improve your ways.

I hope the minister will improve his attitude and do the job that a Minister of Finance ought to do in these matters and encourage members of the house in the performance of the duty that rests upon all members of the house, government supporters as well as the opposition, to scrutinize all government estimates of expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have been criticizing you for not doing it.

I will give you chapter and verse where I have done it, and received small thanks from the minister for doing it. However, if the minister wants to carry on a dialogue, I suppose we shall have to adjourn and find another vehicle for continuing the dialogue.
Mr. Speaker, do you remember these words:
If the order of reference is not wide enough and does not go far enough I suggest to the minister that it should be widened. This is something new; it is an experiment. If in the government's mind it is a reform let us treat it as reform and see that it is properly framed so that it operates. If it is only a concession to my hon. friends of the opposition then let us make our concession freely and willingly, not grudgingly.
And further:
Nevertheless the control, criticism, and scrutiny of the estimates is one of the bulwarks of the opposition. The opposition should, if it is doing its duty, take every possible step to see to it that these expenditures are appropriate and in the interests of the country. May I say as one who enjoyed being in the opposition for two parliaments that I have great sympathy for the opposition, and believe it is the duty of the government and the house to give the opposition every opportunity to scrutinize these estimates.
Mr. Speaker, you will realize that those are not the words of any member of the present government. Those are words uttered by the former hon. member for Quebec South, now Senator Power, in speaking in a debate in this house on February 8, 1955, on the first motion to establish the committee on estimates. Those words will be found at pages 953 and 954 of Hansard of that year. I commend them, for their sound common sense

and ripe parliamentary wisdom, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and those associated with him.
The resolution now under debate is, to all intents and purposes, the same as the one which was submitted by the government on February 8, 1955 and again on February 28, 1956. It is true that there are some words added at the end relating to the provisions of standing order 67(1), but that has to do simply with the number of members serving on the committee. In its essence and in its powers the committee is to be precisely the same as that which sat in the sessions of 1955 and 1956.
I do not need to remind the house-and I am sure I do not need to remind the Minister of Finance-of the fact that for years I have been one of the really enthusiastic advocates in this house of the appointment of a committee on estimates. Long before the government acceded to this proposal in 1955 some of us had been advocating it for years. Notwithstanding the not too satisfactory experience with the 'limited committee that we have had in the past two sessions, Mr. Speaker,
I am still a believer in the necessity for an effective committee on estimates to be set up by this house. It should not be set up as a special committee. It ought to be a standing committee of the house and it ought to be a regular feature of the legislative program of every session that the committee should be established, that it should be appointed early in the session and that it should be set to work with adequate powers to conduct a thoroughly effective scrutiny of the estimates and to obtain all information that the committee deems to be essential for the discharge of its duty.
There is no more important function discharged by this House of Commons than that of the control of public expenditure. There are matters of high importance in legislation. The matter of preserving a correct relationship between government and the elected representatives of the people is also of the highest importance. But no function of parliament is more important than that of the control of public expenditures. After sitting in this house now for 12 years my firm conviction is that in this respect this House of Commons does not effectively discharge its duty.
Part of the difficulty is attributable to a lack of adequate machinery for the purpose. By and large the country must still depend upon the functioning of the committee of supply for the discharge of parliament's duty to control public expenditure. That committee is one of the clumsiest features of all our House of Commons machinery, being a committee of the whole house consisting of

265 members, if they all wish to attend, carrying on under a procedure which effectively prohibits the obtaining of information directly from sources within the department except through the minister himself. Sometimes the minister is a satisfactory vehicle of information; sometimes he is not.
The committee of supply has not effectively discharged its duties. Indeed, by its very nature, it could not effectively discharge it. It is too big. It is too clumsy. It has not the opportunity of bringing necessary witnesses or officials before members to be questioned by them. It is for that reason that the committee on estimates or a committee like a proper committee on estimates is needed. There is undoubtedly useful work for such a committee to do. But if it is to function effectively and to discharge its important responsibility, the committee must have powers commensurate with its responsibilities. This committee of the 1955 and 1956 sessions has not had powers adequate to discharge the responsibility of effective review and scrutiny of the estimates of such departments as have been referred to it for that purpose.
Last year, when a similar motion was introduced we in the official opposition introduced two amendments, one in the same terms as that which is now under debate by which we propose that the committee should be given power to send for persons, papers and records. Surely that is a minimum of power and authority to be given to such a committee if it is to make even the barest pretence of giving effective scrutiny to government estimates of expenditure. The government is still opposed to clothing the committee with such powers. I may say that such powers are given to every standing committee of the house without question and that it is our almost invariable practice to confer such powers upon any special committees that are set up by the house. Yet for some reason or other this committee, which is charged with a responsibility which is no less important than that with which any other committee of the house is charged, is denied these minimum and essential powers. It just does not make sense, Mr. Speaker, and it does not suggest on the part of the government any sincere desire to make this committee really effective for the purpose of scrutinizing government estimates of expenditure.
The other amendment which we introduced last year was one which would have given to the committee broader powers to select the departments whose estimates it should review and not be confined simply to those selected by the government. The government opposed that amendment also as it opposed the other one.
Committee on Estimates
We are making here today, Mr. Speaker, an earnest plea to the house to make this committee really effective and to give it powers necessary for that purpose. Such powers are badly needed if it is to discharge the kind of responsibility that the Minister of Finance today seems to suggest that the committee ought to assume.
I now wish to make a brief reference to several of the matters mentioned by the minister. I realize that these are subjects that have been discussed frequently both in the house and between the minister and myself, certainly in the committee on rules for several sessions.
First of all is the matter that he mentioned or that other members mentioned, namely the burden that is created for members by the establishment of such a committee. Unquestionably this committee has not relieved the house of a great deal of its responsibility or its burden in connection with the detailed review of estimates of expenditures. The review in the committee has in some cases taken quite a good deal of time. One cannot say that that review has resulted in any appreciable reduction of the time that the house found it necessary to devote to the same departments in committee of supply when the estimates were returned to the committee of supply by the committee on estimates. However, I will say this. Such discussion as ensued in the committee of supply was a more informed discussion as a result of the information which had been garnered in the meetings of the committee on estimates by members who applied themselves to their duties in that regard.
Then there is the matter of saving time. I am sure that hon. members would be glad to find a more effective way of reviewing the estimates.
It would commend itself to them if at the same time a more effective procedure could be combined with the removal from the house of the search for extraneous details or abstract matters or items of information which might be gathered up in the committee and presented to the members of the house when they sit in committee of supply in the form of a report or in the report of the proceedings of the committee. That is important.
It is an unfair charge which the Minister of Finance has made today that time was wasted in the committee or occupied unnecessarily while members of the committee pursued political will-o'-the-wisps. That is not a fair statement. If the Minister of Finance will take the trouble to read the report of the minutes and proceedings of the committee last year and will take the trouble to

Committee on Estimates review in particular the pages devoted to the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare he will see that a great deal of time was taken up, not by anything extraneous but by interminably long speeches by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). The Minister of National Health and Welfare is always a pleasant companion and he was usually a most pleasant member of the committee. He added not a little to the good humour of the committee, but 1 will say that he added greatly to the length of the record of the committee. If the Minister of Finance has time to spare I invite him to read some of the perorations which his colleague delivered in that committee. If he does that he will not find it difficult to decide that a great deal of the time of the committee was spent in that way. I am sure he is not surprised at that observation.
Then there is the suggestion which the minister made this afternoon that members of the opposition really wish to use this committee for fishing expeditions. If the purpose of the expedition is to obtain information which will add to the sum total of necessary information on the part of hon. members of this house so that they may do their duty and scrutinize government estimates of expenditure, then there is no time wasted and the expedition has a very salutary effect. A fishing expedition is justified if it has for its purpose the more effective discharge of duty by hon. members in scrutinizing government expenditures and government estimates of expenditure.
I wish to say again, sas I have said I am sure to the weariness of hon. members of this house on past occasions, that there is much in the experience and accomplishment of one of the standing committees of this house to guide us in this matter. I refer to the standing committee on external affairs. That committee has not been denied the power to send for persons, papers and records. It has had that power and it has not confined itself in its review of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs over the last twelve years to the officials of the department. It has gone outside, although not widely; nevertheless it has gone outside. There is not an hon. member of this house who would dare to say that the reference of the estimates of the Department of External Affairs to that standing committee has not been a good thing for the committee, for the department concerned and for the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Was it not as result of setting up that committee that my hon. friend moved that certain other expenditures should be made?
Would the minister elaborate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My understanding is that my hon. friend recommended to the committee certain expenditures that were not being made.

I do not know to what the minister is referring because I certainly have not recommended expenditures. If the minister will look at the record of the committee he will find that I tried desperately hard to get some reductions. I wish he would take the trouble to read last year's proceedings where, for instance, he will see reference made to the extravagance of the government in connection with its acquisition of embassy property at Rio de Janeiro and my efforts to expose its wastefulness in connection with expenditures on furnishings for that building and others. He will see also a record of my amendments which were voted down in the committee. I commend a reading of that record to the minister because I think he will find it instructive. It would help to clear his mind of the mistaken impression under which apparently he is labouring.
That committee is not denied the power to send for persons, papers and records when it is reviewing the estimates of the Department of External Affairs. By what logic then does the government say that the committee on estimates ought to be denied the power to send for persons, papers and records? There just is no sense talking as the minister did this afternoon. The minister referred to talking from both sides of the mouth at the same time. If he wants an example of talking from both sides of the mouth at the same time he should look at the record of the government in this particular, a government which does not cavil at all about giving to the committee on external affairs the powers to send for persons, papers and records but which stands here today and says that the committee on estimates ought to be denied that minimum power essential to its own effectiveness.
Mention was made of the quorum and the matter of assembling a quorum in the committee. I have been a member of the committee in both years for part of the time, according to the practice of rotating membership on the committee as the estimates of different departments are brought before it. In my experience I have not observed any difficulty in obtaining a quorum, but if any such difficulty has been experienced at any time it is certainly not peculiar to this committee and is certainly not peculiar to any party in the house. On the contrary, that is a difficulty which all committees of this house seem to encounter.
I will tell you one or two reasons why I think we encounter that difficulty. One is

that we need very badly a complete recasting of the committee machinery of this house. We have many committees, some of which have not met for years. There are committees of this house which could effectively assume the task of reviewing the estimates of particular government departments associated in their interests with the subject matter of such committees. There are other committees that are needed but are not established. That is one thing.
Another factor is that we have not yet- and here the government must bear the principal responsibility-adequately arranged the business of the house so that we are spared the annual experience of having a whole lot of overlapping in committee meetings late in the session. We have this experience every year and every hon. member of the house knows it. I have had the personal experience of being expected to be in four different places at the same time, in the house and in three different committees. No hon. member can pretend that that is a satisfactory situation, nor can it be said that it is an unusual experience. I hope the time is coming when those who bear governmental responsibility, who bear the responsibility for the leadership of this house and of the government will take serious note of this problem of arranging the business of the house so that we have not a multiplicity of conflicting committee meetings proceeding simultaneously.
Another problem with respect to this particular committee is that it holds so many of its meetings while the house itself is in session. One has seen situations where hon. members find it absolutely necessary to be in their places in the house and for that reason are not able to be in their places in the committee.
I mentioned earlier that last year one amendment introduced by the official opposition, one which it was my privilege to introduce, sought to give the committee itself the power to select the departments whose estimates would be reviewed. I think we made a strong case to the house in the light of the long experience at Westminster for giving to the committee that power. As it is now, there is no element of surprise anywhere in the selection of the departments whose estimates are to be referred to the committee. Nothing is left to the wisdom or experience which the committee has gained in this regard. No, the departments whose estimates are going to the committee are selected by the government here in the chamber, and the committee has no voice whatsoever in the selection of the departments which it is to review.
The estimates committee in the United Kingdom was established 45 years ago. It
Committee on Estimates has attained a degree of effectiveness that the kind of cbmmittee the Prime Minister is proposing here today can never hope to attain. There the committee is given an infinitely freer hand in the selection of the department whose estimates it is to study. It has power to divide itself into subcommittees, and it has five subcommittees. It operates suddenly. It does not necessarily go through the estimates of a whole department; it may select a particular branch of a particular department. It may select a crown corporation or some government agency, and call the officials of the department or agency before it with very little notice.
Government control in a matter of this kind is, in my submission to the house, to be deplored. This is one area in which parliament should seek to proceed without any interference or control on the part of the government, because it is the estimates of government departments that we are seeking to scrutinize more effectively by means of the committee on estimates. How can it be expected that that work will be effectively discharged when the government itself selects the particular work that the committee is to do and maintains a stranglehold upon such business as will be permitted to go before the committee together with this denial of effective powers to the committee?
I recall that when the committee was set up two years ago the minister was frank enough to say it was an experiment. We have now had an opportunity of observing this experiment for two years, an experiment with a limited, truncated committee, a committee with inadequate powers, having no control over the business that is to come before it. Sir, the time has come to carry the experiment a step forward and say that now we shall really give this committee a fair opportunity. The time has come to carry it further by giving the committee powers adequate for the purpose for which it was set up; by giving it, at least, the power to send for persons, papers and records, and to invest it with some measure of control over the work it is to undertake.
We are functioning in this house, today, Mr. Speaker, with virtually the same machinery as was set up immediately after confederation, when our estimates, our government expenditures, were just one-fifth of one per cent of the expenditure this year. Expenditure by government since those days has multiplied five hundredfold, and yet we are going along with the same creaking, old, inadequate machinery as was used then. Surely in the face of the need for doing an effective service in the interests of the people of this country by scrutinizing all those

Committee on Estimates estimates efficiently, the minimum we must do now is to give this committee on estimates adequate power so that it may thoroughly and effectively undertake this task.
Some of us have had a feeling that the Minister of Finance himself does not disagree -could not disagree-with the point of view put forward by the opposition with regard to this matter in their effort to make the committee really effective, but that he has been restrained by some of his colleagues who just do not like the idea of anybody having any better opportunity to scrutinize their estimates. Surely this experiment has now advanced to the point where it should be given a really fair opportunity.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I turn to that other matter with regard to which the minister directed some taunting remarks this afternoon in the direction of the official opposition. This is the matter of finding the waste, the task of eliminating wasteful expenditure. One would have thought, listening to the minister this afternoon, that the members of the official opposition had not approached this task, even within the very limited powers of this committee, with a determination to find waste wherever it might be exposed and, having found it, to eliminate it.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the government's antagonism with regard to giving this committee powers adequate to enable it to do effective work in this respect seems to stem from the antagonism which the government shows at all times toward any effort to bring about any elimination of waste or extravagance. They are always on a very belligerent defensive, a very offensive defensive, whenever matters of this kind are raised in the house; and because the minister is evidently not aware of the efforts of members of the opposition on that committee to bring about a reduction of expenditure, I am going to invite the attention of the Minister of Finance, with apology for the circumstance that this is a motion with which I was associated, to the fact that an effort was made in that committee to bring about the elimination of a quite unnecessary estimate of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I refer the minister to page 252, and following pages, of the proceedings of the committee last year.
He will find there that I brought in a motion to chop $100,000 off the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare in the appropriations for what is euphoniously called "educational and informational publicity" under which the minister would have been given still more money that he had expended the year before, for even with the most resolute determination on his part to make full and effective use of everything parliament placed at his disposal he

had not been able to spend nearly as much as parliament had voted in that year. Yet he came back asking for a very large amount, $631,000, for this purpose. I tried to reduce that by $100,000, which would still have left him with a great deal more than he had expended the year before.
But did I receive any encouragement from the minister? Did he say, "This is a commendable effort on the part of the opposition to assist the Minister of Finance in his task of reducing expenditure and eliminating waste"? No. One encountered the same unvarying attitude which the government, and members who support the government, always display; a bristling hostility to any suggestion that any member of the opposition should propose the elimination of unnecessary and wasteful expenditure.

Mr. Speaker, I point to the proceedings of the committee on external affairs, and remind the minister of other occasions on which I brought in motions to reduce the estimates. But one never receives any encouragement; one never encounters anything but bristling hostility. The Minister of Finance comes here and in the most pleading tones summons all members of the house to assist him in finding waste, in finding all this water that is to be squeezed out of the estimates. He tells us that he himself has burned the midnight oil in such efforts, and is, generally, overflowing with good intentions in this regard. Well, Mr. Speaker, I wish he could communicate to his colleagues in the house some of these pious claims to virtue in this respect, for so far as my experience is concerned I have encountered nothing but inveterate hostility on the part of the government whenever one seeks to reduce so much as a single estimate in an endeavour to curtail waste or extravagance.
What is needed is some continuing machinery. Mr. Deutsch, in the article that has

been mentioned this afternoon, draws attention to the need for something in the nature of an annual review. He has, in this article, pointed directly to the fact that the multiplication of boards, commissions and crown companies has had the effect of establishing what he calls "a high degree of administrative independence from parliamentary and political control." Then he quotes this remark of Professor Laski at page 570:
Everyone with the least acquaintance with government cannot but be aware that there is a give and take between every minister and his chief officials which makes the latter unseen partners, as it were, in the purposes he seeks to implement.
Mr. Deutsch adds, "It cannot be otherwise." He says that in drawing attention to the need of supplying to the opposition all possible assistance and all information to enable them to discharge effectively their duty in the matter of control of public expenditure. In' looking over the present machinery and the present practice he says:
Because of the advantageous position of the executive in these respects, the frustration of parliament is further aggravated.
In the light of that penetrating comment by Professor Deutsch I wish to say that what the government is seeking to do in opposing this necessary amendment is to aggravate further the frustration of parliament, at which they have proved themselves so adept and ingenious in the past.
On the matter of the need of an annual review I quote a short passage from Professor Deutsch's article. At page 572 he says:
One step to this end, which would be in harmony with the principles of our parliamentary system, would be the development of a procedure for a regular annual review of the administrative operations of government by a suitable parliamentary body. Under this proposal a committee of the House of Commons on which there is wide representation, possibly the existing public accounts committee with some modifications, would bring before it each year-
I emphasize those words "each year".
-during the course of the session, all of the permanent civil service heads of departments and agencies to give an accounting of their administrative operations during the previous year, and to submit to examination thereon.
There is much that the public accounts committee might be able to do in this regard although it is difficult there to come to grips with matters that are so stale as matters are by the time they have reached the public accounts committee, both due to the arrangement of our fiscal year and the time that elapses before the Auditor General has completed his report for the next following year. But, sir, what is required is machinery created for an annual review.
Committee on Estimates
It may not be possible-in fact, it is quite evident that it is not possible-in one committee to review all estimates of all departments in one session, but there are other committees that could be associated with the committee on estimates for that purpose. But it is undeniable that no committee can pretend to discharge effectively the tasks that are being laid on this committee unless it is given powers of review adequate for the purpose; and I say, sir, at the risk of repetition, that these powers must include the power to send for persons, papers and records.
Therefore, sir, I say in conclusion that our amendment will undeniably increase the usefulness of the committee, that the power we ask the house to confer upon it is a power with which the house clothes every standing committee of the house and which it is the invariable practice of the house to confer also upon its special committees. The committee should have the power to send for officials. It should also have the power to seek advice in the public interest outside the public service on matters where that advice would be useful. Therefore in putting this amendment before the house today we are seeking to give the house the opportunity to discharge, really effectively and thoroughly, this high duty of scrutinizing the estimates of public expenditure.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have ever risen to speak on a divorce bill. I have not spoken in the past because I think our divorce laws are archaic and barbaric and that they should not be handled in the House of Commons and in the other place anyway. However, if we are going to continue to handle them, then I do think there should be an insistence on decency and correctness in the evidence upon which a divorce is granted.
In this particular bill Francoise Yip Lim Lesage is asking for a divorce and, in accordance with the rules, she had to submit and did submit a petition to the other place. It is interesting, first of all, in reading the petition to note that Francoise Yip Lim Lesage humbly sheweth:
That on or about May 24, 1956, In the city and district of Montreal, in the province of Quebec, the said Marcel Lesage committed adultery; and that adultery was committed at about 5.15 a.m. at the Campus hotel in Montreal, by the respondent and a woman unknown to your petitioner.
The first interesting point to me is that the petitioner knows the exact hour and the exact minute of the adultery, but she does not know the date. It strikes me a little bit peculiar to start off with. But the petitioner appeared before a subcommittee of the divorce committee and gave evidence. In the transcript of evidence, of which we all have a copy, she is asked a question by her solicitor, a well-known lawyer in the city. The question is to be found on page 10, and is as follows:
Q. You allege in paragraph 6 of your petition that your husband committed adultery with a woman unknown to yourself on the 24th of May, 1956. Do you have any personal knowledge concerning that act of adultery? A. No.
Q. You allege this as a result of what you have been told by others. Is that right? A. Yes.
So in the evidence we have the admission that as far as the petitioner is concerned she has no knowledge of the adultery, but now it comes out that the date is the 24th. We have to proceed to the evidence of the person who gave the petitioner the tale of the adultery, and there are two of them. The first is an investigator by the name of Gilles D'Avignon. Under oath this man is questioned by the solicitor. He is asked the date on which the adultery took place, and his answer is found on page 11 of the transcript as May 25. If you turn over the page you will find in the transcript a question asked two minutes later by Mr. Wright as to the date that he saw the adultery take place, and he says that it was on the morning of May 26. Therefore we have in this one case of one charge of adultery the dates of May 24, May 25 and May 26.

Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 15 which is now before the house has as its purpose the proposal to divide each of its 5 million shares into five shares so the company will be set up on the basis of 25 million shares without nominal or par value. It was pointed out by the sponsor of the bill, and this information is also contained in the explanatory note, that the shares of this company have gone up considerably in price. Indeed, they have gone up from an initial price of $10 to a price of about $115 or $120.
The sponsors of this bill contend that the high price of the shares at the present time inhibits trading, and also that it discourages investment by so-called little people. The expressed desire therefore is to divide each of the shares into five, on the theory that the price of the new shares will be one-fifth of the price today, a result which it is supposed will have the effect of encouraging more people to invest in Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company.
I am sure it is no secret that stock splitting is usually proposed as a means of making money. The hope is, and it is a hope based on experience in other instances, that when shares worth $115 to $120 or $130 are broken into shares worth one-fifth that price there will be more trading on the market and that the price of the new shares will likewise move up so the holders of all the shares, whether on the old or the new basis, will profit as the result of such a transaction.
In the speeches that have been made by other members of this group we have already

pointed out that we feel that the real purpose of this legislation is to enable those who already are making money out of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company to reap further profits. I confess that we do not accept as the real reasons the reasons stated by the people who came to parliament and asked for this bill.
When Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company first came to parliament in 1951 and asked for an act of incorporation, we were told that the initial shareholders were Mr. S.	D. Bechtel of Oakland, California; Mr. S. M. Blair of Bolton in Albion township, Ontario; Mr. I. G. Wahn, Toronto, Ontario; Mr. A. D. McAlpine of Toronto, Ontario; and Mr. R. L. Bridges of San Francisco, California.
One does not know whether those five gentlemen are still shareholders, although there is evidence that some of them are. Indeed, I believe it is reasonable to assume that all five of the gentlemen whom I have named are still shareholders of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. I make that point for a reason I shall give in a few minutes. According to the 1957 version of "Western Canadian Oils", which includes the "National Gas Review" published by James Richardson and Sons, the officers and directors of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company are as follows:
President, D. M. Morrison Secretary, J. H. McQuarrie Treasurer, R. F. Taylor Assistant secretary, E. G. Sheasby Assistant treasurer, K. M. Leask Administration manager, E. C. Hurd Operations manager, E. S. Davis
Those are the officers, according to the information contained in the bulletin to which I have referred. I find that the other directors of the company are:
W. M. V. Ash, Toronto, Ontario R. D. Baker, Burnaby, British Columbia R. L. Bridges, San Francisco, California E. D. Day, Los Angeles, California J. W. Hamilton, York Mills, Ontario J. K. Jamieson, Toronto, Ontario I. G. Wahn, Toronto, Ontario W. J. Wilkins, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
I put those names on the record because I think it is reasonable to assume that they are all shareholders in this company, namely Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. I think it would be interesting to note a few facts about some of the gentlemen who are shareholders in this company. S. D. Bechtel, who was one of the original shareholders mentioned in the act of incorporation in 1951, is on the board of many corporations in the United States, including among others J. P. Morgan Co. Inc., Continental Can Co., and so on.
Mr. R. L. Bridges is a lawyer who is connected with Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line

Company and Alpac Construction and Surveys Limited. He is a director of Canadian Industrial Corporation; Oregon Shipbuilding Corporation and Panama Pacific Tankers Inc. He is director and general counsel of Bechtel Corporation of San Francisco.
Let us take another one. R. D. Baker of Burnaby, British Columbia, is president and managing director of the Standard Oil Company of British Columbia. He is a director of Crown Zellerbach, Canada, Limited; Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company; Alpac Construction and Surveys Limited and White Pass-Yukon Corporation Limited.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: What has this to do with the bill?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
My hon. friend has asked a very good question, to which I will come in a moment. Let me say to my hon. friend that I am simply laying a basis for what we believe to be a major point so far as this bill is concerned. I welcome the interest of the hon. member for York-Scarborough.
Mr. J. K. Jamieson is another of the gentlemen listed, and I find he is vice-president and a director of Imperial Oil Limited. He is of course a director of Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company as well as of Alpac Construction and Surveys Limited, Portland Pipe Line Corporation and Esso Research and Engineering Company.
I think I have made it clear that the gentlemen who are shareholders in this company, the gentlemen who are asking that the shares be split five ways, as a result of which they will stand to profit, are gentlemen who are pretty well set up in the financial and economic affairs of the United States and Canada. They are not exactly needy citizens; yet the effect of this bill and this sharesplitting operation that parliament is being asked to endorse will be to put extra profits into the hands of those people.
If anyone were so bold as to come before parliament with a bill proposing an income tax or any other kind of tax on the people of Canada for the purpose of turning over additional money to these well-fixed gentle-ment whom I have named he would be laughed out of this house. Yet that is the proposal now before us; that is what this bill does. We have tried to point this out on a number of occasions, but our friends in all the other three parties in this house are either unable or unwilling to grasp this fundamental economic fact, namely that a profit which is taken out of the economy of this country and put into the hands of certain people is just as much a tax on the gross national product as
Private Bills
is the kind of taxation imposed by the Minister of Finance by way of income tax, sales tax, corporation tax or what have you.
My hon. friends in the other three parties are always ready to complain when we ask for an expenditure which we feel is justified but with which they are not prepared to go along because they contend it means a tax on the taxpayers of Canada. Our point is that the sweat and toil of the workers and farmers of this country, the production that comes from the toil of the workers and farmers of this country is taxed just as surely by transactions of this kind that drain off profits as it is when the Minister of Finance levies taxation by legislation in this house. My friends in the Social Credit party fail to understand that, as do those in the Liberal and Conservative parties.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: How do you know they fail to understand it?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Because when I enunciated this principle yesterday my hon. friends in the Social Credit party applied some epithet to it which was not exactly parliamentary. We pointed out that when people like Mr. Bechtel and Mr. Bridges and the gentlemen we were talking about yesterday are able to drain off great wealth by stock transactions, that wealth comes out of the gross national product of this country and is just as much a tax on what our people produce as is any tax imposed by the government of Canada or the government of any province.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Can the hon. member explain just why a stock split, which is all the bill contemplates, would drain off huge profits for the shareholders concerned? It is merely a method of reducing the denomination so market transactions by those who wish to purchase smaller amounts of shares in smaller denominations will be facilitated.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: It is just as simple as that, says the hon. gentleman. Does he not realize that so far as the promoters are concerned the purpose of splitting these shares and getting them down to smaller denominations is so that in trading on the stock market the new price will again start to climb with the result that the shares will be valued at still higher prices?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: How does that work out in the case of a decline in the market price?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
These companies do not ask for a splitting of shares when a decline is in prospect. Stock splitting is asked for when an increase in the price of the shares is in prospect, and hon. members opposite know that is precisely why this is being done. That is the history of these shares. Their

Private Bills
value has gone up from $10 to $115, or whatever the figure is now. Maybe it is a little higher than that. These gentleman have reason to hope that if these shares are split so they are valued at around $25, the new price will climb as the result of trading to $50 or perhaps $100 again, thus resulting in increased holdings in the possession of those who own these shares.
Does the hon. member for York-Scar-borough imagine that these profits come out of thin air? Surely he knows that money does not grow on trees. Surely he knows that profits do not come out of thin air. Surely he knows that if there are pieces of paper, money or cheques in the country which indicate a certain total amount of wealth, they have value only if there is behind them real production of goods and services. And if you give to some of the people in our country or, as in this case, to people in another country as well, claims on the wealth that is produced by the workers and farmers of this country, I say again that you are taxing our workers and farmers; you are taking away from them a portion of the wealth they produce as surely as if taxation had been imposed by the Minister of Finance.
We feel that this is a source of confusion in this country. People get all worked up and hon. members of this house get all worked up about the imposition of taxes by the government, but some of the people who complain loudest about taxation by the government, or who complain if taxation resources are spent in certain ways rather than in other ways, are indifferent when by means of this other process a real tax is imposed upon the gross national product, which means that just that much less of the gross national product is left for the workers, the farmers, the old age pensioners and others. That is a different story; and when we express our opinions about it we are told we are trying to smear these people, or the people we were talking about yesterday.
It is nothing of the kind. We are asking for social and economic justice. We are asking that when the workers and farmers of this country produce real wealth they should get it back. The Minister of Finance said today that the C.C.F. party favoured high taxation, and favoured taxation as a means of redistributing wealth. I did not interrupt him on that point, because I took what he said as said in good faith. What he meant was that we favour reasonable taxation for the purpose of distributing wealth, and we do. But this, Mr. Speaker, is unreasonable taxation for the purpose of getting a corner on some of the wealth which the workers and farmers produce so it will get

into the hands of people who happen to own these share certificates, people who now want their certificates split five ways so their value will be further enhanced.
So, Mr. Speaker, because in our view the purpose of this bill is other than as stated in the explanatory note appended to it by the company that brought in the bill, we feel that it should not be passed by this house. That is the reason why there is an amendment before you, moved by my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo, that the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject-matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I think I should make at least a passing reference to an article which appeared in the Financial Times under date of February 22, 1957, entitled "The Stock Option Battle, or: Who is making Money?" I mention this article because it happens to refer to a "Nation's Business" broadcast over the television network which was made a short while ago by my leader, the hon. member for Roset'own-Biggar. The writer of this article, Mr. E. J. DeSeau, begins by saying, "Oh dear, somebody has been making money again." Of course he goes on in that fashion and suggests that we in this party fail to understand the situation because we do not like it when a few individuals make private gain out of the work and the toil of the population as a whole.
The reason I mention this article in particular is that the writer referred to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar as having made a mistake when he said that the stock of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, which insiders got at $10, was selling at $130. May I point out, Mr. Speaker, as one who heard my leader's broadcast over the television network and as one who has seen the script used on that occasion, that he was not referring at that time to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. This was before certain new items had appeared which we discussed yesterday. Rather he was referring to this company whose application is now before us, namely Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company, the price of whose shares has gone up from $10 to $130.
Well, we say to the writer of this article, who does not like our criticism of this kind of transaction, that' we do not complain because people are making money or because people as a whole are making wealth. That is what we want for our people out of the economy of Canada. We want all the people of Canada who work and toil to get the wealth, to get the goods and services, to get

the better standard of living which they have made possible by their labour and toil. But when we are confronted by this kind of thing, which drains off large portions of the wealth which our people produce, we rise up and object as we are doing with respect to this bill.
I accept the statement made by the Minister of Finance earlier today, that we do not object to reasonable taxation by the people themselves through their government for the purpose of redistributing the wealth of our people, creating social security benefits and so on. But we do object to this unreasonable form of taxing the gross national wealth which our people produce, for the benefit of a few such as those I have named in referring to some of the shareholders of this company.

Mr. Speaker, just before this
debate was interrupted by the hour that has to be devoted to private and public bills, I was pointing out that the Leader of the Opposition had referred with approval to the terms of the resolution proposed as a private members' resolution by Hon. Mr. Lemieux in April, 1921, as reported at page' 2193 of Hansard for that year. Had the hon. gentleman turned to the response made by Sir Henry Drayton 10 pages farther on he would have seen the demonstration by Sir Henry Drayton that the proposal was quite contrary to the constitution. Sir Henry Drayton cited what he said was a very excellent authority, Colonel A. J. V. Durell, in his book "Principles and Practice of the System of Control over Parliamentary Grants".
May I ask the Prime Minister the page number?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Page 2203. The writer discussed the pros and cons and then had this to say:
The most obvious way for securing parliamentary control over the estimates is that a select committee should examine them in detail before they are presented and while they are still in a stage where reductions can be made on non-party lines without such proposals being considered as motions adverse to the government, as is the case when the estimates have been presented to the house as the policy of the government.
But he goes on and adds:
Any procedure of this sort, however, strikes at the root of the fundamental principle of ministerial responsibility.
A little farther down he says:
Another authority . . . declared that the adoption of a proposal to submit the estimates to a committee for preliminary examination and approval before presentation to the house would diminish the proper responsibility of the executive for the public expenditure and would interfere with the constitutional relations between the government and the House of Commons. The duty of the House of Commons is to decide whether the expenditure which the various departments propose is absolutely needed for the efficiency of the public service, and to see that all money is wisely spent and that the nation gets the full equivalent for the outlay. The latter duties are post mortem and may safely be delegated to the public accounts committee without the breach of any constitutional principle being involved.
He goes on:
By the English arrangement of examining the estimates, ministerial responsibility is increased as the proposals which form the ensemble of the budget are altogether the work of the cabinet, whose liability is undivided . . . No proposals subversive of this important fundamental principle of the constitution could be embodied in any scheme for securing closer parliamentary control

and it was for this reason Gladstone did not proceed in the matter when considering the possibility of referring the estimates to a committee to be gone into as a matter of business.
The discussion went on and Hon. George Foster also took part in opposing the proposal. In the course of his remarks he was asked by Mr. Mackenzie King if that objection would not be eliminated by substituting for the terms of the resolution the words "the estimates of the various departments should, after being laid on the table but before being discussed, be scrutinized by a special committee," and so on. Sir George Foster went on to discuss that saying that was not practical in his view under our constitutional system.
It will be said that for a number of years the British parliament has adopted a system of a committee on estimates which selects some one particular thing and investigates it in the manner described this afternoon by the Minister of Finance. Sometimes these investigations require a long voyage to Africa to examine peanut fields. In other cases they require trips through the United Kingdom and so forth. However, the hon. gentleman will know that under the British system there are a certain number of days allotted to the consideration of the estimates, and when those days have expired all the remaining estimates are adopted in the block without any consideration at all being given to the various items which make up the block.
Under the British system there is no written constitution and parliament can depart from the practice if it sees fit. We have a written constitution which expressly provides in article 54 of the British North America Act:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue or of any tax or impost to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or bill is proposed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that not just the same as the British system in every particular?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is the same as the British system by tradition at the time the British North America Act was passed, but it is within their power to depart from that tradition if they see fit to do so, while it is not within our power to depart from the terms of the written constitution. That is the law under which we have to operate, and which makes it necessary to do as is done, to bring down estimates with a recommendation of His Excellency the Governor General on the responsibility of 82715-107
Committee on Estimates the government, and of all the ministers, for each and every individual item recommended in those estimates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

They still bring down their estimates, but they can adopt the procedure to deal with them as they see fit, without being required by the written determination of a written constitution to follow any special procedure. It is for that reason it is not possible to have the system the hon. gentleman seemed to be recommending this afternoon, on the strength of a resolution proposed in 1921 by Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux, to have the estimates considered with the officials who make the recommendations to their ministers before they are presented as recommendations of the crown on the responsibility of the government.
I was asked if there is anything unconstitutional in what is being done by the committee on external affairs. I do not think there is. But the hon. gentleman knows that in the committee on external affairs the policy of the department in its diplomatic relations with the rest of the world comes up for examination, whilst on the general estimates the officials have no part of the responsibility the cabinet has to take for the recommendation of the estimates that are placed before parliament.
I do not think it would be a good practice to bring forward the officials of the department and ask, "Now, did your minister follow your advice in making up the estimates for his department that then went to the treasury board for scrutiny, and very frequently for reduction, before they were brought before the house?" When information is being sought about facts it is quite all right to get those facts, and they have never been refused. Committee on Estimates before parliament. The purpose of this amendment is to find out whether the officials of the department agree with the conclusions their ministers reached after they had given them their advice.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is not so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Our view of constitutional government is that we require the best advice we can get, but that after having received that advice we take the responsibility for decisions, and those who want to remain public servants are then required to carry out the decisions that we take. We do not wish to have the system that prevails in a neighbouring country where officials are brought before the committee of the House of Representatives or the Senate to try and maintain opinions they may entertain different from those that form the conclusions of the heads of the departments; because there, as hon. gentlemen know, the members of the cabinet are responsible only to the President and the President is responsible to public opinion. He has no special responsibility to the House of Representatives or to the Senate and they are not competent to dismiss him from office, as this House of Commons is competent to dismiss us from office if we do not make the kind of decisions that are satisfactory to a majority of those who represent the electors who have sent them to this House of Commons.
That is the system which had gone on before 1921 and since 1921, and I think the results of every government that has been in office have been results with which the Canadian public have reason to be satisfied.

speechtext: What is the difference between the estimates committee dealing with estimates which are on the responsibility of the ministers and, let us say, the banking and commerce committee dealing with a bill which has been referred to it and which is the responsibility of a minister? authority to send for officials of any of the departments to ask them whether their opinions agree with that of their minister.

May I ask the Prime Minister a question? What is the objection on the constitutional basis, having regard to the system of parliamentary government, when what we are proposing is something that has been in effect at Westminster in the mother of parliaments for the last 45 years.

speechtext: Whether it has been in effect in the mother of parliaments for 45 years or not does not change the article of the Canadian constitution which was adopted in 1867.

That a select committee to be designated be appointed to consider such of the estimates as may be referred to it and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house, and that the provisions of standing order 67(1) limiting the number of members on special committees be suspended in relation thereto.
