"and that the said committee have power to send for persons, papers and records."
For the life of me, Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand what we are arguing about. What we are proposing-as I understand it, it has not been contradicted by the Prime Minister or anyone else-is exactly what has been done in the Department of External Affairs for twelve years. I believe the Prime

Minister does not contradict me. I have listened to the constitutional argument, and I shall not undertake to go very far into constitutionalities with the Prime Minister; but this I can say. The last thing in the world we are trying to do on this side is to deny the principles of responsible government. I think we understand them. We have plenty of reason to understand them; we have plenty of evidence of the fact that responsibility is in the cabinet, with the support of the majority in this House of Commons.
We do understand the difference between that and the United States plan where, as I understand it, the President prepares the estimates and sends them across so to speak, to Congress, and Congress can deal with them pretty freely. Then they are sent back to the President and as a matter of practice, as I understand it, it usually happens that the President, in order to get the thing done, gives way. At any rate they arrive at a working arrangement. If it were not that they are sensible people with practical views they might run into difficulties, but they get them through.
So far as we are concerned, the present Leader of the Opposition and his predecessors have stated again and again that we recognize the principle of responsible government. We are not trying to infringe upon the responsibilities of the cabinet. What we are asking for is information.
I come back and say I do not yet understand what we are arguing about. All that is here are three words, "persons, papers and records". If what the Prime Minister described was really happening, if we were trying to get civil servants to put them into a position of embarrassment by trying to find out whether there was a difference between them and their ministers, then I would say the Prime Minister would be quite justified in feeling critical about the suggestion.
The Minister of Finance can contradict me if he wishes. He mentioned this afternoon that his estimates had gone through fairly quickly; I think he said, "in three hours".
I was not quite sure whether he was giving us praise or blame for that. Whether we were sensible people, in his opinion, for accepting the work of himself and his colleagues so quickly, or whether we were not doing our duty, I was not quite sure. At any rate, my recollection was that there was no difficulty there. My recollection is that we did not run into any violent disputes. I think the fact that it was done in two or three hours probably proves that fact. Maybe figures speak for themselves. Maybe figures are more impersonal than the subject matter of other 82715-1071
Committee on Estimates committees where there were some differences. But I come back-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would my hon. friend then admit that, in so far as the examination of the Department of Finance was concerned, the committee was a success?

Mr. Speaker, I would want to go back and look through the records and see whether there were points of dispute. However, I do not remember any at the moment. On the other hand, I remember very well that there were points of dispute in the other committees. The reason I raise the question on finance is that it may be that some of the other ministers should be inoculated by the Minister of Finance. I do not know whether or not there is anything in that.
I should like to come back again to the committee on external affairs. As my colleague the hon. member for Eglinton reminds me, it has been carrying on for 12 years. That is not just a fly by night experiment; that committee has been going on and there has been no suggestion-and I repeat this, Mr. Speaker-there has been no suggestion that I have heard that it is not working properly and effectively. No constitutional difficulty has arisen and the thing has worked out, as I say, effectively.
I think in general one would be obliged to admit that a small committee is more efficient than is a large committee. I was a little bit slow to come to that view, but my colleague the hon. member for Eglinton I think persuaded me. We have tried this committee and, surely we agree.
In the second place, surely we also agree that there are things which need to be improved. There is no doubt about that. We had an instance where that was brought out not so long ago, in the autumn of 1955, by a writer in the Winnipeg Free Press who pointed out the tendency for government departments just to multiply themselves without much critical sense being applied to the matter. I am not going to bother with that quotation now because I cannot lay my hand on it.
I want to come quickly to what was said by Mr. Deutsch, and perhaps that is the reason I am speaking at all. I want to put on the record two things said by Mr. Deutsch. He seems to me to have introduced a new element into this situation, that is to say the idea that there is a duty on the members of this parliament to concern themselves with the efficiency and enormously increased scope of government operations. Some of the things he says reminding us of the increase in the scope of government operations

Committee on Estimates I am going to put briefly on the record because I think it is desirable that anyone who happens to read Hansard should know something about it. I confess that I was amazed to realize the increase in the extent of government operations from the way he has them summarized here. On page 567 of the Queen's Quarterly of December last we find this:
In order to help provide an ever widening horizon of economic opportunity the federal government nowadays conducts investigations, studies, and research into a vast number of problems. To illustrate the scope and complexity of these activities it is not necessary to do more than to refer to such diverse efforts as those being made to improve the techniques of farming, forestry, mining and fishing; to discover the causes of disease in men, animals and plants; to eradicate pests and scourges; to apply the advances in basic scientific knowledge to the tasks of lightening the burdens and discomforts of life . . .
And so on. Farther on I read the following:
In the field of direct service and production the federal government operates gigantic transportation and communication systems, huge mortgage and credit schemes, marketing facilities for one of the country's basic exports, and a large complex chemical plant. Each of these is among the biggest businesses in the country. Related to all this, is an extensive organization for the gathering, compiling, and the publishing of facts and statistics concerning an immense range of economic and human affairs.
Then he goes on to say that the difficulty confronting parliament lies essentially in the problem of how to control this vast machine. He refers to the difficulty confronting parliament. I sometimes wonder whether we give enough consideration to the fact that parliament has a responsibility in this matter. I read further from the article, as follows:
The difficulty confronting parliament lies essentially in the problem of how to control this vast machine, including the executive which directs it. Parliament itself has recognized the increasingly technical and discretionary character of the activities of government in the growing amount of delegated legislation which has been put on the statute books.
I read again as follows:
In many cases parliament has gone further and has created special administrative devices in the form of boards, commissions and crown companies precisely for the purpose of establishing a high degree of administrative independence from parliamentary and political control.
If we needed to be reminded of it, we were reminded the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he told us that it was not proper to discuss a certain subject in this parliament because it was being considered by a committee of civil servants. That shows the extent to which parliament has been shoved into the background. I want to go on and read briefly, because it has already been mentioned and I think it is extremely important. I shall read again part of what
[Mr. Macdonnell.l
Mr. Deutsch says. He speaks about the necessity of parliamentary action, and he says this:
It is necessary somehow to bring parliament more closely in touch with the modern realities of government operations and the work of the civil service.
I believe all members of this house will agree that is so. I suggest that is one of the things we are trying to do, and that it is merely good sense. Then he goes on to say this:
One step to this end, which would be in harmony with the principles of our parliamentary system, would be the development of a procedure for a regular annual review of the administrative operations of government by a suitable parliamentary body.
I am not going to read more because I think part of it was read this afternoon. At any rate we have here an entirely new and, to me, extremely important consideration introduced, not merely the scrutinizing of certain expenditures which are put before us and which we do more or less well, but the idea that we, the parliament of Canada, have a tremendous range of business which is being conducted in our name and that we cannot just sit here and passively take a bunch of figures without trying to know more about them.
Why is this objectionable? With deference I suggest that the Prime Minister attempted to confuse it in a mass of what I thought were irrelevant constitutional points. I think that was a great pity. I think this is a very simple matter. As I say, it is still difficult for me to see why we cannot agree about it. We have in effect agreed about it. I have already said that we are not questioning the principle of responsible government. We would be silly to do that. We believe in it. We live by it. We hope one day to be discharging these duties ourselves. Incidentally, I should like to go back to what Mr. Lemieux said, as reported on page 2194 of Hansard of April 18, 1921, on the page following the one at which appears the resolution to which the Prime Minister referred. He said:
My motion does not propose the alteration of any essential, any elemental principle of the constitution. Of course, in the matter of expenditures the initiative must and always will rest with the executive.
I accept the embarrassment of finding that two previous leaders in my own party appear to argue in some ways against that proposition. But that is what I believe and that is what we believe, namely that we are not infringing on the constitution in any way, that we are not attempting to cut down or tamper with the principles of responsible

government. I find it difficult to know why the ministers are unwilling to let us talk to civil servants.
We are not suspicious of the ministers' honesty; we simply want to be informed further. To me there is something inexpressibly tiresome in having to have information come through a conduit pipe, or having a kind of curtain drawn between us and the people who have the information. When we sit here in the House of Commons in committee of the whole we recognize the fact that civil servants talk in undertones to the ministers and the answers come to us in that way. Surely one advantage of having a small committee would be that we could get away from that procedure.
I do not want to get into controversial things and I should like very much to believe that it is possible to agree on this, but as a matter of fact I suppose one has to try to realize the reason the ministers do not want to give us information. I suppose it must be because of their exercising power in a big way and getting used to it. I remember during the war there was an article in that leftist journal the New Statesman. They were discussing the giving out of military information. They recognized that a certain amount of military information had to be carefully rationed because of security reasons.
We too recognize that there may be security reasons or the equivalent of security reasons that would apply not only to the Department of Defence but to other departments. The writer of that article went on to say that he recognized that there might be information which should be withheld, but on the other hand he believed that a lot of bureaucrats, a lot of people in authority, would say to the public, "You want to be informed about that; parliament wants to be informed about that. Well, damn it, they won't be."
I feel that perhaps unintentionally a certain amount of that spirit has developed simply because we in the opposition want things; therefore we cannot have them. I come back to where I began. I cannot for the life of me see why in the light of what has happened in connection with the Department of External Affairs an amendment which asks for persons, papers and records cannot be accepted. Let us get on with the matter.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to support this amendment I should like to remark that the Minister of Finance has not given the house any good reason why we should not be authorized to send for persons, papers and records. While the Prime Minister dealt with this at some length, I think he made a very weak argument. When a similar resolution was before
Committee on Estimates parliament two years ago Senator Power, then the member for Quebec South, made a most constructive speech. Unfortunately it was one of the last speeches he made in this chamber. I should like to quote from page 953 of Hansard for February 8, 1955, where the then member for Quebec South is reported as having said:
With respect to the procedure in the committee, it would appear that all parties seem to be in agreement on one thing anyway, namely, that policy is the business of the government and the responsibility of the minister, and that officers of the department should not properly be questioned on matters of policy.
I think all who have spoken have assumed that to be correct. The former member for Quebec South then went on to say:
Now, coming to the procedure in the committee, I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) that the business of carrying on by whispering or sotto voce suggestions will be impracticable if not futile in the narrow confines of a committee room. Pretty nearly all the members of the committee will hear the replies that the deputy minister whispers to his minister and naturally the members of the committee will say: "Well, Mr. Minister, ask him this or ask him that", which would be a sort of three-handed form of questioning which would finally finish up by being a bit ridiculous.
I would say that there should be nothing in the order of reference nor in the intentions of the government to preclude officers of the department from being examined and cross-examined. But I would say this: If any minister believes that he on his own can answer all the questions which an ingenious opposition can put to him, well, then, let him try it.
And later on:
With respect to hon. members on the government side, perhaps it should be said that there is no constitutional or legal bar to their scrutinizing the estimates also. Such scrutiny is not by law, practice, or the constitution the sole prerogative of members of the opposition.
And again:
From the standpoint of the government I can think of no better procedure than to have deputy ministers appear before parliamentary committees. Anyone who has been in the government must be aware of the almost intolerable pressure brought upon ministers to increase the estimates of the departments whether it be the natural tendency to empire-building which exists in all departments and which is very difficult to control; whether it be the pressure to have new gadgets in departmental offices; or whether it be only keeping up with the Jones's in some other department, the ministers have only one way of protecting themselves against this pressure from their officials and that is to be able to say, "No, I cannot get by with this in the House of Commons." If the departmental officers are brought face to face with members of the house and made to understand the reluctance of members to give in to their whims and fancies, then perhaps the minister would have a much easier time with his department. Without being derogatory in any way to our civil service, I think it would be a good idea to match bureaucracy face to face with democracy as represented by the members of this house.
I submit that those words of advice from a former member of the cabinet should

Committee on Estimates register particularly with the backbenchers on the government side. I think the arguments which have been made by those who have tried to get the government to accept this minor amendment after two years' experience are reasonable. This afternoon the Minister of Finance mentioned that his estimates went through the house last year in about three hours. Like the hon. member for Greenwood I do not know whether the minister was criticizing or complimenting the house for disposing of his estimates so quickly.
I think all of us must recognize that this year we are about to consider estimates running to over $5 billion, which is more than ten times the amount parliament considered just prior to world war II. I think we all have to re-examine the procedure we have followed of sometimes spending hours on items which appear to be quite trivial and then, as the minister pointed out, putting through the estimates of the Department of Finance in one brief session.
I notice that this year the minister is asking for $52 million for regular expenses and well over $1 billion authorized by statute. He is asking for $163 million more than he required a year ago. I submit that disposing of items such as the one covering the administration of the Bank Act, the very large items for public debt charges, subsidies and other payments to the ten provinces, the tariff board, payments to municipalities, contingencies and miscellaneous, and items to provide for the Gordon commission and the royal commission on Newfoundland, superannuation payments-disposing of all these important subjects in three hours is not good enough.
I think, with all due respect to the Minister of Finance and to all the other ministers, that it is worth while continuing this experiment which was begun two years ago; and I believe in the light of our experience we should be given a chance to have the officials appear before the committee.
I have only served on the one committee, the committee which studied the estimates in connection with the Department of National Health and Welfare, and I would like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that this committee apparently acted in a manner contrary to the terms of reference. We had General Worthington before the committee, and the business of asking questions of General Worthington through the minister and General Worthington replying through the minister became, as Senator Power suggested, somewhat ridiculous.
One of the members of the committee asked the minister if any of the officials


had been to Sweden, and the minister replied, "Yes, General Worthington has been there three times." Then the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said, "Is it possible to hear from those who have visited Sweden?" To this the minister answered, "I have no objection if you would like to hear General Worthington on that subject". The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said, "I think it would be most interesting". Then followed a very interesting description of what our civil defence co-ordinator had seen with his own eyes in Sweden.
I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare will not be censored by his colleagues in the cabinet, or by the house, for suggesting that we ignore the terms of the reference from the house. I am sure the members of the committee were not interested in trying to find out whether there was any difference of opinion between the minister and General Worthington. On the contrary, I think they were interested in finding out what is being done in civil defence, and with all due respect to the minister I suggest he would not have been able to have given the committee the information which was given by General Worthington. I am sure that should the Minister of Finance have his estimates before the committee certain members of that committee may wish to discuss with officials of his department the effect the tight money policy is having on our whole economy. And while the minister is a very outstanding lawyer, I think he would not be able to discuss some of the problems which would be of importance to the committee, just as the Minister of National Health and Welfare was not able to tell the committee the story that one of his officials could tell.
So, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that this committee contains an overwhelming majority of government supporters who are invariably on hand to see that the government is not unduly embarrassed, I would hope that this amendment which we have before us might be accepted, and that the committee might have power to send for persons, papers and records.

that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to implement a convention between Canada and the United States of America for the protection, preservation and extension of the sockeye salmon fisheries in the Fraser river system, signed at Washington on the 26th day of May, 1930, and a protocol thereto signed at Ottawa on the 28th day of December, 1956, and for carrying out Canada's obligations under the said convention and protocol.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution will introduce a measure which has been long and eagerly sought, and is now strongly endorsed, by the whole fishing industry of British Columbia, the fishing companies, the fishermen's union, the fishing co-operatives and the native brotherhood. The bill which will follow will extend the jurisdiction of the international Pacific salmon commission to include control over and regulation of the pink salmon of the Fraser river watershed in line with an agreement signed last December by the government of Canada and the government of the United States.
The international Pacific salmon commission has had an extraordinary record of achievement in restoring the sockeye runs of the Fraser river, and our fishing industry knows that this commission, with its skilled band of scientists and officers with 20 years' experience in salmon management, can do an equally good job in restoring the pink salmon run of this area. This is the first time the international salmon commission has been open in the 20 years this commission has functioned, and there are one or two minor amendments which have been found advisable in view of the experience which has been garnered by the commission over these years.
I intend to speak at some length on second reading of this bill to outline the actual achievements of the international salmon commission in restoring this very valuable resource, and to discuss the program they intend to follow in managing the pink salmon fishery. I think members will be able to follow that better on second reading, because

Fisheries
they will then have the bill in their hands and will know exactly what is proposed. After second reading I propose to refer this bill to the standing committee on marine fisheries so members can question our technical experts on every phase of it. We are anxious to have this bill approved as soon as possible in order that the salmon commission can begin to exercise control over these fisheries during the coming season. I might add that President Eisenhower has asked his congress to give speedy approval to the bill which he has submitted to congress.

subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, never have truer words been spoken than when the minister said, in effect, that legislation to take care of the conservation of our pink salmon on the Pacific coast has been long overdue and has been eagerly awaited, not only by the fishing industry but by the fishermen. In fact for years now the fishermen have been pleading that the pink salmon, which are spawned in our Canadian streams then take to the ocean until they are adult, when they return to these same streams again should be available in fair proportion to Canadian fishermen when they are passing through the waters approaching the Fraser river, where they are caught by United States and Canadian fishermen.
It would seem, however, that for some reason or other the government has been unwilling to take the initiative in introducing such legislation until very recent times. Of course the United States government was not the least bit interested. For years their fishermen have been catching 65 per cent or more of the salmon which have been passing into the Fraser river. Our Canadian fishermen did take such measures as were available to them in order that they might have something approaching a fair share of the Canadian fish. The result was that there developed a cutthroat competition during recent years between United States and Canadian fishermen in the straits of Juan de Fuca and along Puget sound. In order to get ahead of the United States fishermen in Puget sound our fishermen had to go farther and farther out to sea. The result of this move was a need for bigger and more expensive equipment, bigger and more expensive gear and longer hauls. It was an uneconomic process, because not only did larger fishing vessels have to be provided, but floating camps had to be sent out to service that fishing fleet.
Then again, the fish are at their prime when they have finished feeding in the ocean and just before they enter into the fresh water and start to live on their oils and fat. The fish are not at their prime when they still have food in their stomachs.

This resolution, therefore, is welcome. It is welcomed, as I said, by the fishing industry, the fish boat owners and by the fishermen. The federal government has the sole responsibility for looking after our fisheries. In some cases this responsibility may be delegated by the federal government to the province. So far as fishing on the Pacific coast is concerned, however, that is the responsibility of the federal government. The federal government has been interested. I am glad to say there has been a growing interest in conservation measures.
The minister referred to the international pacific salmon fishery commission. Yes, there has to be co-operation not only between the industry and the governments, but where you have fishermen of different countries catching the same run of fish, there has to be co-operation between the governments of the different countries. This is very much the case with the British Columbia salmon because, as everybody knows, the British Columbia salmon be they sockeye or pink spawn in our rivers. After the eggs have been hatched some species move at once to the ocean, while others require time in fresh water to develop, and like the sockeye spent two or three years in a fresh water lake before proceeding to the ocean. But as soon as the pink salmon hatch they move out to salt water, and after they have become adult fish and are full grown after approximately two years, they return to those streams where they were hatched.
The Fraser river is the great salmon river of this continent, and the approaches from the ocean to the mouth of the Fraser must be either around the southern end of Vancouver island or around the northern end of that island and down through the Johnstone straits and so to the mouth of the river.
It has been, as the minister says, very largely as a result of the international commission that was set up under the sockeye salmon fisheries convention of 1930, which arranged for the equal division of the catch as between the United States fishermen and the Canadian fishermen, and also an equal division of the responsibilities for the research work and the general development of the sockeye run to the Fraser river, that the Fraser run has been rebuilt. That result was brought about by the painstaking efforts of the international salmon fisheries commission.
I think everybody on the Pacific coast will speak with enthusiasm of the efficient and effective work which has been done by that commission. It consists of a board of some six men, three from Canada and three from the United States. They have been impartial

in all their findings, and have won the respect of the fishing industry and of the fishermen of both countries. Therefore it was only natural that when at last it was considered desirable to take steps to conserve the pink salmon on our coast, the responsibility not only for conserving the pink salmon but also for stopping the competition which had existed, and dividing the share equally between the fishermen of the United States and of Canada in a way similar to what had been done with the sockeye salmon, should be given by the governments of Canada and the United States to the international salmon commission in order to supervise that work.
People sometimes wonder as to the difference between the pink and the sockeye salmon. The sockeye is perhaps better known, and because of its popularity in the past the importance of the pink salmon industry has been largely overlooked. Let me give hon. members some idea of the importance of our pink salmon. The last figures I have for 1955 show that in the area which now will be conserved, that is the area of the approaches to the Fraser river, 63,160,000 pounds of pink salmon were landed. The landed value of that fish was $5,617,000 and the marketed value, after they had been processed, was $15,953,000.
I mention that just to indicate the importance of the measures which will be introduced and the importance of our pink salmon industry; but I am not certain that this importance is fully represented even by those figures, because the pinks are becoming more and more important, and there is every indication that in the future they may even surpass the sockeye in importance.
Let me give one indication of the growing development and the changes which are being brought about in an effort to adjust the conflicting interests of salmon and power in our British Columbia streams. Experiments have been carried out at Jones creek, which is a small stream between Chilliwack and Hope, in locating in artificial spawning beds pink salmon spawn from other beds. The important thing is that the fry of the pink salmon proceed at once to the ocean, and therefore there is not the long delay that is required for the fry of the sockeye salmon to become fingerlings. The result is that the pink salmon may be relocated. It is hoped that it will be possible to replant the spawn in other streams than those required for power purposes and in streams which do not have fresh water lakes readily available, which are so essential for the sockeye spawn.
I think we should bear in mind that there are other species of salmon such as chum,
Fisheries
cohoe and spring. This treaty or agreement which will be introduced as a result of this resolution does not cover any conservation measures for these other species of salmon, although reference is made in the protocol to the fact that there is to be a six-year study of the movements and habits of the pink salmon, and that while this study is taking place the commission is to report on the habits of other species of salmon.
I should like to emphasize the importance of that study. I hope it will be pressed with vigour, because it would seem there is reason to believe that in the course of a few years, and after further study, it would be wise to include at least the chum salmon in a similar convention with the United States.
I quote from the salmon spawning report of 1956. In the first paragraph the Department of Fisheries states:
For the second consecutive year, outstanding feature was the serious decline in the chum run to most sections of the coast.
Then in a subsequent paragraph it goes on to state this:
Despite special protective measures, chums destined for the Fraser were seriously reduced in number during passage through Johnstone straits the Discovery passage by the highly efficient and mobile seine and gillnet fleets there. Other important chum reproduction areas, in common with the Fraser, also suffered from the effectiveness of this fishing operation. These included generally the streams along the east coast of Vancouver island below Seymour narrows as far south as Chemainus river as well as on the mainland streams opposite, including Jervis inlet and Howe sound. Further measures to provide for an adequate progressive escapement through this fishery are imperative immediately.
I am not suggesting that we should include the chums in the present protocol. I am only urging that special attention be paid during the next six years in order to ascertain the movement of the chum salmon, with the prospect in view that it may be desirable then to make some treaty which will include a fair distribution of the chum salmon. The chum do not move through the straits of Juan de Fuca and Puget sound in the same proportion as do the sockeye and pink salmon. There is a considerable run of chum salmon coming around the northern end of Vancouver island and down through Johnstone straits and so approaching the mainland rivers.
Of course nobody is going to suggest that those salmon which move entirely through Canadian waters should in any way be shared with the fishermen of the United States. But still there are numbers of chum that move through the international waters of the strait of Juan de Fuca. I think that fact makes it important that further study should be given to the movement of the chum salmon before any final decision is reached.

Fisheries
I understand that the bill, when presented, will not only be discussed in committee here [DOT]-and the minister has said that he is going to make a more complete statement on second reading-but that it will be referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries. There are certain sections in connection with the protocol which I feel should be discussed at that time, and which would probably be better discussed there than here at the resolution stage.
I shall conclude by stating that I feel that the objectives of this convention are wholly commendable. It is desirable that this great natural wealth in our fish should be preserved. As a result of the success of the commission it is evident that this end can be achieved best of all by combining the efforts of the two countries concerned and working through the medium of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, which has proved to be so efficient in its administration of the sockeye run.

it at that time and, if I may, I would like to read briefly from the speech made by Mr. Neill in this house on March 25, 1937. This is from page 2191 of Hansard of that date. He said:
Mr. Chairman, I would like first to thank the government, and more particularly the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who I think was leading the house when he agreed to bring this matter into the house at the request of myself and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). It is no lack of modesty that leads me to put my name before his, but simply because I brought it up first by a question in the house and then on the orders of the day, and I suffer no least illusion as to what my fate would have been if it had not been for the powerful intervention of the leader of the opposition. I have only to look at the answer that I got to the question which I asked on March 3, when I was told that the reservations or understandings simply constitute clarifications or interpretations upon administrative aspects and therefore it was not necessary to bring them into the house. That, Mr. Chairman, is another illustration of the ever-growing custom in this house, not under this government alone, but under preceding governments as well, of proceeding to eliminate almost all the power and influence of the ordinary common member and giving us government by cabinet rather than by parliament.
I could not help but think when I read that last sentence I quoted from the former member for Comox-Alberni that it had a somewhat familiar ring, when one thinks of some of the things which have been said during this current parliament.
The reason I quoted that part of Mr. Neill's speech was to indicate that had he not raised the matter at that time the house would not, apparently, have gone through even the formality of passing a resolution giving its approval to this protocol of exchange of ratifications, nor would we have been provided with much indication of what the will of parliament was in respect to that protocol which is now referred to in this present addition to the convention.
Mr. R. B. Bennett, then leader of the opposition, summed up the situation rather well, I think, and actually put the case that I feel I should like to place before the house at this time when he said-and I am quoting from page 2183 of Hansard of March 25, 1937:
I do suggest to the Minister of Justice that it would be desirable, from the standpoint of maintaining uniformity of practice, that a short bill should be prepared on the basis of this resolution ratifying, in the terms of this resolution, the three understandings in question. I suggest that only in order that we may maintain uniformity of the practice and procedure which we have initiated in connection with this treaty.
The position may be summarized in a few sentences. A treaty was approved by this parliament by a chapter of the statutes of 1930 and now there has been a modification of it-I will leave out the words "understandings" and "reservations" and use the generic term "modification". That modification is comprised in three paragraphs that are now before us, and I suggest, in order that our position may be consistent, that we should now say,

in terms of the statute, that we are accepting the new offer, and enact it as a statute of Canada, supplementary to the statute which we passed in 1930.
That is the end of the quotation from the remarks which the then leader of the opposition, Mr. R. B. Bennett, made on that occasion. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that while we are at the resolution stage of this discussion it would be appropriate to draw to the attention of the house the existence of what I feel is a rather unsatisfactory situation, particularly in view of the fact that the present protocol makes specific reference to these understandings which, as I have previously indicated, are not in any formal way attached to the convention documents as far as I have been able to ascertain.

subsubtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, together with other hon. members who have spoken with respect to this particular resolution I am indeed very happy and pleased that the minister has been able to negotiate with his United States counterpart the possibility of bringing the pink salmon under the agreements of the international Pacific salmon fisheries convention.
I must agree with the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat in respect to the manner in which the Minister of Fisheries has conducted his office, more particularly in regard to this matter. It was my pleasure to be present at a meeting at White Rock on April 17, 1955, at which certain of the remarks of the minister were brought to the attention of the fishermen's delegates from both the United States and Canada, remarks in which he is supposed to have indicated a desire that the Canadians should out-fish the Americans, and suggested that would bring them to some form of reason. At the time, the fishermen's union and many of the fishermen expressed the view that it was a dangerous undertaking, and I myself admit I was somewhat perturbed. However, the gamble paid off and it was probably well taken at the time.
I must say that in the matter of the conservation of the pink salmon industry it has been my privilege, as the minister will recall, to draw this question to the attention of the house, as the hon. member for Fraser Valley and many others in this chamber have done, and impress upon him the need for government action.
At the meeting to which I alluded earlier, Mr. Chairman, the minister and the house will recognize, I am sure, that not only the Canadians but the Americans, too, were quite in agreement.
I was very pleased to hear the hon. member for Comox-Alberni read what was apparently a press dispatch indicating that

fishermen in the state of Washington had passed a resolution agreeing to the inclusion of pink salmon under the jurisdiction of the international fisheries Pacific salmon commission to the tune of 92 votes to none.
The importance of the pink salmon industry and the fishing industry generally is emphasized to a considerable degree in the preliminary report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. In reading the report I was quite disturbed to find that while the commission recognized the value of the industry to Canada, they offered very little in the way of suggestions with respect to doing something about conservation in the industry. Certainly the fishing industry has proved to be very necessary to the economy of the country, because I find in the report of the commission that some two-thirds of the income from our fisheries is derived from exports.
In my own province of British Columbia the production of the fishing industry is valued today at some $60 million or more, and the fact that two-thirds is exported is of great significance in helping to balance our trade with the United States, something that seems to be so necessary to our economy today. Our fishermen are doing an excellent job in helping to keep our country stable so far as the balance of trade is concerned.
The value of the sockeye salmon commission and the work it has done in past years cannot be stressed too strongly. I am very pleased that the work of the commission has taken such a routine form that they find they have the time to take under their wing the pink salmon industry as well. Inasmuch as they have done such a good job of the conservation of sockeye salmon they should be in a position to expand their work. Certainly with the experience they have had I do not think we can find a better body to which to refer the particular task we are setting out for them.
The minister indicated in his earlier remarks that it was his intention to refer this matter to the marine and fisheries committee. I feel that is very important in the case of this legislation, because it will definitely give us an opportunity to discuss the various aspects of the legislation that now exist and possibly get a more basic understanding of the problem of the fishing industry, more particlularly with respect to the application of the legislation to the industry in British Columbia.
There are many problems of conservation of fish in the Pacific region. Some of them
Fisheries
were outlined by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. Certainly there are others, not the least of which is the question of the terms of reference so far as the committee itself is concerned. I listened with a great deal of interest to what the member for Esquimalt-Saanich had to say about the spawning of salmon up the Fraser river. I am fully aware of the small acreage required for the actual spawning grounds, but we do have a problem there that requires considerable attention; and whether the authority of the Pacific salmon commission now extends to the point where we might have a greater degree of control over some of the other factors affecting conservation is something that might well be studied when the bill goes before the committee.
There are certain factors having to do with the Fraser river itself and the part it has played in the conservation of the salmon industry. The fact is, as the minister well knows, that a good number of the fishermen within the area above the Pattullo bridge are fully aware of the problem that faces them in trying to remain in the fishing industry, when at the same time they are being deprived of a good number of fish that they rightfully consider their own. I am thinking more particularly at this moment of the fact that Canadians have made a habit of conserving the salmon while the Americans have depleted the run. That is just one phase of the question.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to call it 10 o'clock.
